A customer identity that holds no membership gets `403` from every business endpoint and reaches only `GET /api/me/account-state`, exactly as a workforce stranger does.

**Nothing is linked, duplicated or inherited by mailbox.** Identity linking stays deferred (#713), so a local account that registers an address an existing member already uses — through a work account or through Google — is a new actor with no membership, no role and no inherited access, and presenting its token writes no membership row. A duplicate registration of one address is a second directory object and therefore a second actor. An email change or a password reset at the provider changes no `(tid, oid)`, so it can neither move nor widen a membership: the same pair resolves the same business and role whether the token carries a different address, an unverified one, or none at all. The `NoMembership` welcome page is where this is explained, and it now names an email address beside the work account and Google.

**A failure says one of two fixed sentences.** A refused credential journey is where "no such account" leaks, because the provider's own error text names the mailbox, the directory and often the reason. `classifySignInFailure` reduces a failure to *cancelled* or *failed* from the provider's error **code** alone, and only those two application-authored sentences are rendered, so the page never discloses whether an address has an account here and never shows provider text.

**No new configuration, and the same rollback lever.** Journey D needs no identifier, flag or setting beyond issue #710's `ExternalId` section and issue #711's `externalIdSettings` — it is the same tenant, registration and flow — so clearing those settings removes both journeys at once (design § 15.1), and a deployment no human has configured shows no customer identity action, says nothing about passwords, and signs in exactly as it did before. Everything that makes the journey *work* is human portal configuration: enabling email with password inside the user flow, its verification and self-service password reset, and the available anti-abuse and MFA controls — see [README.md § Signing in with an email address and password](../README.md#signing-in-with-an-email-address-and-password-issue-712) for the recorded control set, its verified gaps (no built-in bot or sign-up fraud protection, no built-in per-IP throttling) and the staging checks a human performs.

**What proves it.** `auth/sign-in.component.spec.ts` pins the single action's label, the hosted-flow line, the registration/verification/reset help line, the absence of any `input` or `form` element on the page, that a deployment with no customer identity tenant says nothing about passwords at all, and that a refused sign-in renders one generic sentence and never the provider's description, account name or error code. `auth/sign-in.service.spec.ts` pins the exact keys of the redirect request. `access/welcome.component.spec.ts` pins that the separate-accounts explanation names an email address. On the API side, `TrustedIssuerTokenValidationTests` adds four regressions: a local account sharing a member's mailbox inherits nothing and gains no membership row, a second registration of one mailbox is a second actor with nothing of the first, neither an unverified nor a verified mailbox claim reaches a business endpoint on a direct API request, and a member's changed, unverified or absent address decides nothing about their membership.

#### Verifying the customer identity rollout (issue #714)

Issues #710, #711 and #712 each proved their own piece. This is the consolidated validation of the whole rollout, and the thing it is most careful about is **what a passing build does not mean**. [docs/identity-rollout-verification.md](identity-rollout-verification.md) is the document of record: the verification matrix, the staging smoke tests, the phased enablement, the observability signals, the incident and rollback procedure, and the production go/no-go checklist.

**Three kinds of evidence, declared per row and never pooled.** A *synthetic API/JWT* test says what the API accepts, refuses and resolves for a given token. A *synthetic browser journey* says what the SPA decides, stores, refuses and asks MSAL for. Only a *human hosted-provider staging run* can say that a tenant exists, that a provider is enabled inside its user flow, that the application is associated with that flow, and that a real token carries the claims the design assumes. Each row is `passed`, `failed` or `not verified`, and the automated suites cannot produce the third kind of evidence — which is why `docs/identity-rollout-verification.md` § 2.6 lists every hosted-provider row as **not verified** and § 7 treats that as blocking.

**What the automated half covers, and where it lives.** `backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/CustomerIdentityRolloutMatrixTests` runs the provider × account-state × role matrix through the real pipeline with real tokens from **both** trusted issuers, reusing issue #710's signing keys and stubbed metadata documents so the validation under test is the one that ships: invitation redemption in both directions, the already-a-member `409` that stands in for a linking conflict, every non-member account state reported identically per issuer with `403` from every business endpoint, revocation taking effect on the next request, deactivation ending access and cancelling live invites with reactivation restoring the member's own role, a role granting the same capabilities whichever issuer signed the member in, the whole platform-admin surface refusing a customer identity (T9), and two-business isolation across the issuers (T8). `CustomerIdentityRollbackRehearsalTests` rehearses design § 15's lever 1 over **one database read by three hosts in turn** — configured, rolled back, configured again — so "memberships and outstanding invites are retained and work again when the settings are restored" is asserted as a property of data surviving a configuration change; it also keeps the legacy Super Admin recovery route tested while customer identity sign-in is off, and asserts that a refused issuer, an expired token and a successful redemption leave no bearer token, invitation token or mailbox in the logs. On the browser side, `frontend/inventory-app/src/app/auth/customer-identity-journey.spec.ts` composes the real units into whole journeys: an interrupted invite acceptance through a cancellation and a retry with the token reaching no MSAL request, cache or stored destination; the two authorities sharing no client id, authority or audience while both keep one cache location, so the partition is the client id; a provider switch asking only the newly chosen authority for a token; the § 15.1 rollback lever landing on a tab part-way through; and a destination outside this application never becoming a redirect start page.

**Nothing in the application changed.** This is a verification task: no production code, no configuration default, no contract and no schema is touched by it, and the suites above are evidence rather than behaviour. A test here that fails is a finding about #710, #711 or #712, not about #714.

#### End-to-end testing authentication (issue #46)

There is exactly one exception to the two bullets above, and it exists so the browser-level end-to-end suite can reach protected pages and endpoints without an interactive Entra sign-in — which issue #46 explicitly does not test. Everything about it is in `backend/InventoryApi/Auth/E2ETesting/`.

**The gate.** `E2ETestEnvironment.IsEnabled` is the only way into any of it, and it answers `true` for exactly one hosting environment name, `E2ETest`, compared ordinally. The decision is made from the host the process was started as, before any request exists: no header, query string, route value, cookie or request body takes part in it, there is no endpoint that turns it on, and there is no configuration key that can. A near-miss name (`e2etest`, `E2ETest2`) is not that environment. The `E2ETest` host is a local test host only; it is never deployed, and `deploy-production.yml` deploys the API with its own environment.

**What the host swaps, and nothing else.** `AddInventoryApiAuthentication` (`InventoryApiAuthenticationExtensions`) makes one either/or decision: the E2E host registers `E2ETestAuthenticationHandler` and no other scheme, and **every** other environment — Production, Development, the backend suite's `Testing`, and any future one — registers the real `AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi` bearer scheme this composition always registered — and, in those other environments alone and only when one is configured, the pinned customer identity scheme of issue #710, which this host never gets whatever is configured. There is no public method that registers the test scheme, so no other part of the application can add it to a host. The same gate also registers `E2ETestNayaxLynxClient` (`Adapters/Nayax/`) in place of the real Nayax HTTP client, so the E2E host has nothing configured that could call the live operator account, and `E2ETestFixture` seeds the suite's two synthetic businesses into the disposable database that host was pointed at.

**It authenticates; it does not authorise.** The synthetic principal carries the same `(tid, oid)` claim pair and the same `scp: access_as_user` scope a real access token carries, from a closed, compile-time set of three synthetic actors (`E2ETestActors`). Everything after authentication is the production pipeline: `[Authorize]`, `[RequiredScope]`, `BusinessScopeMiddleware`, the `BusinessMembership` lookup, the tenant query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`. One of the three actors is deliberately given no membership, so the suite proves that an authenticated caller outside every business is refused `403`. The `X-E2E-Test-Actor` header only chooses between those three already-permitted identities, exactly as a bearer token identifies a user; a missing, unknown, blank or repeated value authenticates nobody and the request is answered `401`. The fixture itself never runs unscoped: businesses and memberships are not tenant-owned rows, and every tenant-owned row it writes goes through a `BusinessScope` resolved to one business, so `UnscopedBusinessScope` stays reserved for the three human-invoked commands.

**The frontend half is a build replacement, not a runtime flag.** `src/app/auth/browser-auth-providers.ts` holds the real MSAL wiring (`MSAL_INSTANCE`, `MsalGuard`, `MsalInterceptor`, …) that `app.config.ts` spreads into the application config. The `e2e` build configuration in `angular.json` — and only that configuration — replaces that one module with `browser-auth-providers.e2e.ts`, which lets the router through, stubs `MsalService`/`MsalBroadcastService` so no MSAL call reaches `login.microsoftonline.com`, and registers no HTTP interceptor and therefore attaches no token. A production or development bundle does not contain that module at all, so there is nothing in it to enable.

**What proves it.** `backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/E2ETestAuthenticationCompositionTests` pins the gate and what each environment registers; `E2ETestAuthenticationFailsClosedTests` hosts the real pipeline as Production, Development, `Testing`, `Staging` and `e2etest` and asserts the synthetic header authenticates nobody (`401`), the scheme is not registered, and no fixture data is seeded; `E2ETestAuthenticationTests` hosts the E2E environment and asserts the `401`/`403`/`200` boundary and two-business isolation by listing and by id. `browser-auth-providers.spec.ts` asserts the production module keeps the real guard and interceptor and that the replacement is declared in one build configuration only. All of these run in `scripts/validate.sh`; the Playwright suite itself does not (see [Frontend tests](#frontend-tests)).

### Tenant ownership (issue #64)

Authentication answers "who is this?". Tenant ownership answers "whose data is this?", and the two are deliberately not the same question. An Entra directory tenant is not a vending business: the mapping between them is application-owned data, so the business a caller belongs to is a decision this application makes and can audit, not one inherited from the token.

**Identity and membership.** The actor is identified by the validated `(tid, oid)` claim pair — never by email, display name, or the Entra directory tenant alone, all of which are mutable or shared. Since issue #524 the membership row does *store* a display name and an email address, refreshed from that same validated token, and they are display-only personal data that decides nothing: see [Member display name and email](#member-display-name-and-email-issue-524). `BusinessMembership` rows map an actor to one application-owned `Business`. `BusinessMembershipResolutionPolicy` (Domain) decides the outcome: exactly one active membership on a business whose lifecycle status is `Active` resolves; none, or several, or any other business status, denies — see [Business lifecycle status and profile](#business-lifecycle-status-and-profile-issue-540). Ambiguity is denied rather than resolved by picking one, because silently choosing a business is how data ends up in the wrong ledger. Since issue #522 the database also refuses to *create* that ambiguity, so the resolution denial is the second line of defence rather than the first — see [One active membership per identity](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522).

**Layering.** Claims parsing stays at the API boundary (`EntraActorIdentityAccessor`, the only implementation of the Application's `IAuthenticatedActorAccessor` port). `ICurrentBusinessProvider` is the Application-facing abstraction; `Inventory.Domain` and `Inventory.Application` never reference ASP.NET claims or principals. EF query filters and `SaveChanges` enforcement are persistence concerns and live with the `AppDbContext` adapter.

**Per-request resolution.** `BusinessScopeMiddleware` runs after authentication and authorization and before the endpoint, resolves membership once, and publishes the answer into the request-scoped `BusinessScope`. The resolution is memoised in the request's own scope, so the capability policies that run earlier in the pipeline (see [Capability authorization](#capability-authorization-issue-525)) and this middleware read one membership lookup between them and cannot disagree about the caller's role. An authenticated caller with no usable membership gets `403` and never reaches an action; the response carries no detail about why, because telling an unrecognised caller whether a business exists is information they have not earned. `IBusinessScope` exists as a separate synchronous port because query filters and `SaveChanges` cannot await a membership lookup. Two endpoint markers, and only two, are eligible to proceed without a membership — the platform diagnostics surface of issue #336 and the account-state family of issue #523 — and a request that does carries the same *denied* scope, so neither reads business data; see [Platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336) and [Account state and the membership-not-required marker](#account-state-and-the-membership-not-required-marker-issue-523). One other middleware takes part in a request that presents a support session, and it is deliberately the **outermost** one rather than another step beside this one: `SupportSessionAuditMiddleware` (issue #672) runs ahead of `UseExceptionHandler`, because the trail of what somebody from outside the business asked for has to include the attempts authorization refused above this middleware and has to record the status the exception handler finally mapped — see [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**One other way a business is resolved, and it is not a membership.** Since issue #551 a platform administrator who presents an active support session's id in the `X-Support-Session` header has that session's business published as `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` — the same business key the filters compare against, and nothing writable. It is the third documented exception to "the business comes only from the caller's membership", and it is not an exception to "never from request input": the header carries a session id, which is a credential, and the business is the one the server stored when the session started. Everything about it — how a request joins one, the read-only enforcement in three layers, the fixed capability set and the Nayax block — is in [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**Fail closed.** `BusinessScope` starts denied and can only move forward to a resolved business, once — either an ordinary `Resolved` one or a support session's `SupportReadOnly` one, and never across from one to the other. A denied scope yields a `null` business ID, and the filters compare with `==`, so an unresolved caller matches no row. "No current business" must never be read as "no filter" — that would convert a resolution bug into a cross-business leak. A scope cannot be repointed mid-request.

**Tenant-owned versus global.** Everything persisted is tenant-owned — products, categories, suppliers, purchases and items, stock adjustments, supplier orders and allocations, sales, imports and their children, expenses, commissions, fee rates, costing transition records, each business's own Nayax credentials (issue #518) and report facts — except **five** structural exceptions: `Business` (the boundary itself), `BusinessMembership` (what resolves the boundary, so filtering it would be circular), `BusinessBackfillAudit` (operational evidence about the rollout, which must stay readable precisely when a run assigned rows to the wrong business), `MemberInvite` (the reviewed decision on issue #532: the redemption has to find an invite by the token a caller with no membership presents, and under the denied scope such a request carries a filtered read matches no row at all — see [Invite redemption](#invite-redemption-issue-532)), and `SupportSession` (the reviewed decision on issue #550: every request that reaches it is a platform-admin request, and a platform administrator is a member of no business, so such a request resolves nothing — a filter would match none of its rows and the ownership stamp would have no business to stamp — see [Support sessions](#support-sessions-the-store-and-the-control-endpoints-issue-550)). There is no "global reference data": the enum-like constants live in code as C# enums, not tables. `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` enforces this — a new entity with no ownership fails the build rather than quietly arriving unfiltered — and it asserts the exemption list itself, so a sixth table is a visible edit rather than an addition nobody reviewed.

**"Not tenant-owned" never means "not owned".** Each of the four exempt tables that is not the `Business` itself carries a `BusinessId`, and the boundary for it is that column named in **every** statement over it, by the adapter rather than by the central filter: `EfBusinessMemberStore` and `EfMemberProfileWriteStore` for memberships, `EfMemberInviteStore` and `EfMemberInviteRedemptionStore` for invites, `EfSupportSessionStore` for support sessions. The id is only ever one tenancy resolution produced from the authenticated actor's membership, or — for the redemption alone — the one the invite row itself reports, or — for a support session — the business row the session's own write transaction read; it never comes from a route, query, body or header. (A support session additionally carries the Entra `(tid, oid)` pair it was granted to, and every "my session" statement names that pair, which is the authenticated actor and never a request value.) That is deliberately *not* the per-controller `Where` clause this section warns against: those adapters have no central mechanism to defer to, and each keeps its statements behind one private helper so the owner cannot be omitted on one method.

**Central read enforcement.** `AppDbContext.ConfigureBusinessOwnership` walks the model rather than naming entities: every `IBusinessOwned` type gets a required business key, an index leading with it, and a global query filter. A new tenant-owned entity is protected the day it implements the interface. There is no per-entity list to forget and no controller `Where` clause that could be omitted on one endpoint — which is why adding redundant filters in controllers or services is discouraged rather than merely unnecessary.

**Central write enforcement.** Query filters protect reads only. `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` runs on both `SaveChanges` overloads. Since issue #551 it enforces one rule before the other four: a request in `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` may write **nothing at all** — every table, not only the tenant-owned ones — because in that state there is no write this application wants. The other four rules are about ownership: new rows are **stamped** with the caller's business (callers never supply it); inserts, updates, and deletes of another business's row are **rejected**, which is what stops a detached entity attached by ID from slipping through to an `UPDATE`; the business key is **immutable**, so a record cannot be moved between businesses; and every foreign key between tenant-owned entities must **stay inside one business**. The relationship rule is driven by EF model metadata, not a hand-written list, so a new foreign key is covered as soon as it is mapped. Resolving a principal's owner deliberately uses `IgnoreQueryFilters`, because a principal in another business must be reported as a boundary violation rather than mistaken for "does not exist".

**Tenant-scoped uniqueness.** Constraints over externally supplied values are scoped by business, because two businesses may legitimately hold the same external value: Nayax transaction IDs, import file hashes, site commission agreements, fee effective dates, and costing baselines. `NayaxSales` consequently has its own local key with `TransactionID` unique *per business* — a remote identifier is an external identity, not a primary key. This also keeps import de-duplication correct: one business must never be told its own import is a duplicate because another imported the same bytes first, and a shared remote ID must never cause one business's import to update another's row. The one-active-membership index of issue #522 is deliberately *not* scoped this way, and is not an exception to this rule: `BusinessMembership` is one of the five structural non-tenant-owned tables above, and the value it constrains is an Entra identity that must mean the same person everywhere rather than an externally supplied value two businesses may legitimately share. The invite token hash *is* scoped this way — `(BusinessId, TokenHash)` — even though the invite table is now non-tenant-owned too, because that value is not an identity: a global constraint over it would let one business's row deny another's, and 256 bits of cryptographic randomness is what makes a token unambiguous. The support-session id hash of issue #550 is deliberately the other way round — unique across the whole table — and that is not an exception either: the rule is about values a *business* supplies, and a session id is generated by this server, supplied by nobody, and matched by a request that carries no business to narrow the lookup with, so global uniqueness is what makes "which session is this?" have one answer.

**Protected documents.** A document's bytes live outside the database, so hiding the row is not enough. Retrieval always resolves the tenant-owned parent record first — `GET /api/purchases/{id}/file` and `GET /api/operating-expenses/{id}/attachment` both go through the filtered `DbSet` — and the stored file name is read from that record, never from the request. No endpoint accepts a file name or path as input, and `FileSystemDocumentStorage` reduces any stored name with `Path.GetFileName` and then proves the result is inside the category folder, so a crafted value cannot escape it. Knowing another business's purchase ID, attachment ID, stored file name, and on-disk path therefore yields nothing.

**The unrestricted-context rule.** `new AppDbContext(options)` is fail-closed. Unrestricted, all-business access requires passing `UnscopedBusinessScope.Instance` explicitly, so every such place is greppable. Outside tests it exists only in the three human-invoked commands — `migrate-database`, `bootstrap-business` and `migrate-documents`, the last of which reads every business's document metadata to migrate it (see [Document storage](#document-storage)). Being a human-invoked command is not what grants it: `migrate-nayax-connection` (issue #519) is a fourth such command and constructs no unrestricted context at all, because it needs none — the tenancy tables it reads to resolve the target business carry no tenant filter, and the credential itself is read and written through a context scoped to that one business (see [Migrating the Nayax connection](#migrating-the-nayax-connection-issue-519)). `resolve-nayax-sale-products` (issue #758) is a fifth, on the same pattern: it enumerates businesses through a denied-scope context and reads and writes every sale, product and audit row through a context scoped to the one business that sale belongs to (see [The sale's own product](#the-sales-own-product-issue-758)). No controller, service, or request path may run unrestricted; a composition-root test pins down that the DI container never produces an unscoped context, and issue #544 extended that test to the platform-admin store below — it is registered scoped and its only constructor dependency is the request's own `AppDbContext`, so nothing can hand it anything else. Issue #550's support-session store is held to the same three things, for the same reason: it is the second adapter a platform administrator's denied-scope request reaches. **A support session is not unrestricted either, and is narrower than a membership rather than wider** (issue #551): `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` names exactly one business and is compared by the same filter expression as `Resolved`, so such a request reads that one business and — because `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` refuses every `SaveChanges` in that state — writes nothing at all. See [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551). The platform diagnostics API (issue #336) does **not** change this and is deliberately not implemented with it: a diagnostics request carries a *denied* `BusinessScope`, so the query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` stay in force and it reads nothing at all through `AppDbContext`. Its cross-business read is a separate read-only SQLite connection restricted by SQLite's own authorizer — see [Platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336) for the exception's exact boundaries.

**The one reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` in a request path (issue #544).** The Super Admin's business directory reports whether each business has stored Nayax credentials, `BusinessNayaxConnection` is tenant-owned, and the request carries a denied scope — so the central filter matches none of its rows and the fact is otherwise unreadable. `EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` makes exactly one `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement, projecting `BusinessId` alone, and the rest of the adapter is ordinary reads and writes of the structurally non-tenant-owned tables. It is a *narrowed* exception rather than a loosened rule: the column it reads is the ownership key, not business data, and the alternatives — an unscoped request context, a second read-only cross-business connection, or resolving each business into the request scope in turn — were each strictly worse. See [Super Admin businesses API](#super-admin-businesses-api-issue-544).

**Schema and data are separate steps, and only the data step is exclusively human-controlled.** `DatabaseSchemaStartup` decides per environment: Production, Development, and `Testing` all migrate automatically and fail closed if the attempt fails (issue #201); any other non-Production environment does so only under the `Database:AllowAutomaticMigrationUnsafeOutsideDevelopment` override. Migrations never assign ownership, automatically or otherwise. The backfill is exclusively `bootstrap-business`, run by a human: deterministic, idempotent (it touches only unassigned rows), restartable, transactional, dry-runnable, and verified by before/after counts and financial totals, with a `BusinessBackfillAudit` record of what it did. `TenantOwnershipReadiness` reports at startup whether ownership has actually been bootstrapped, so "all my data is gone" cannot be the first symptom of an unfinished rollout.

**Known limits of this rollout.** One business is live. The Nayax **catalogue** is no longer part of that limit either: its products and categories used to be keyed by the Nayax `NayaxProductID`/`ProductGroupID`, which is one global identifier space, so two businesses could not both import the same Nayax product — issue #735 made a created row's key the database's own and left the provider's id as a per-business column, and `EfCatalogueReviewStoreTenancyTests` proves two businesses importing the same ids (`EfNayaxProductCatalogImportStoreTenancyTests` pinned the same thing for the direct import, until issue #739 replaced it), see [Provider identity on the local row](#provider-identity-on-the-local-row-issues-732-759-and-735). The Nayax **credential** is no longer part of that limit: issue #518 added the per-business storage, issue #519 the human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command that moves the existing credential into it, and issue #520 made the client read the current business's own operator id and token on every call with no global fallback — see [Per-business Nayax credentials](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520). Since issues #536 and #537 an Owner's own credential can also reach the database through the API: a test holds the pasted pair as an encrypted draft and a save promotes it, with a re-test for the stored one — see [Saving a tested connection and re-testing it](#saving-a-tested-connection-and-re-testing-it-issue-537). Since issue #538 an Owner can drive those endpoints from Admin → Integrations, through the connection wizard — see [The Nayax connection wizard](#the-nayax-connection-wizard-issue-538). Since issue #539 every Nayax-dependent screen explains an unready connection instead of failing silently, and points an Owner at the wizard — see [Nayax connection status banners](#nayax-connection-status-banners-issue-539). What is still outstanding before a second business goes live is the rest of #328's self-service work; the business that is live today had its credential moved in by the human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command, which is a human step described in `docs/tenant-rollout.md` § Migrating the Nayax connection into the business. The database foreign keys from `BusinessId` to `Businesses` are a deliberate, still-outstanding deferral — see `docs/tenant-rollout.md`. Issue #39 (document storage) consumes this ownership key and must not introduce blob storage before it.

#### Membership roles and capabilities (issue #521)

Ownership answers "whose data is this?". A role answers "what may this member do with it?", and that is again a separate question: every member of a business sees the same data, and the role decides which of it they may read and change.

**Three roles, on the membership.** `BusinessMembership.Role` is a `required` `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessRole` — `Operator`, `Manager` or `Owner` — stored as that constrained vocabulary's integer value. The values are spaced (`20`, `30`, `40`) so the read-only Viewer role #328 anticipates can be added below `Operator` without renumbering a value that is already persisted, and `0` is deliberately not a declared role, because `0` is what an unfilled integer column and a default-constructed enum both hold. Nothing compares two roles numerically.

**A role is always explicit, and an omitted role grants nothing** (issue #679). The property has no default: `required` makes a creation path that states no role a compile error, so the invite redemption, the self-service application, `bootstrap-business` and the E2E fixture each say which role they mean. `IsActive` is `required` on the same terms — whether a membership grants anything at all is not a value a write should be able to leave unsaid. It used to default to `Owner`, the most privileged role in the business, which is the fail-open shape issue #584 removed from `Business.Status`: a creation path that said nothing got everything. The database half is `RemoveBusinessMembershipRoleOwnerDatabaseDefault`, which replaces the `DEFAULT 40` that `AddBusinessMembershipRole`'s backfill left behind with `DEFAULT 0` — a value no role is declared at — in four in-place statements (add, copy, drop, rename) that preserve every stored role and rebuild no table, the shape `RemoveBusinessStatusActiveDatabaseDefault` established. So an `INSERT` that never goes through EF and names no role now produces a membership that is denied rather than an Owner. `IsActive` needed no migration: that column has never carried a database default, so a row that states no activation fails its `NOT NULL` constraint outright. What the entity still cannot refuse is a *cast* undeclared role — `(BusinessRole)99` from inside the code — which is stored and then denied on every request by the policy below rather than refused on the way in; a `SaveChanges` enforcer for it, on `BusinessStatusEnforcer`'s pattern, is deliberately left to its own reviewed change.

**An unknown stored role denies access.** `BusinessMembershipResolutionPolicy` checks the role of the membership that would otherwise have resolved, and a value this code does not declare — a hand-written `UPDATE`, or a role a newer deployment wrote — is denied as `RoleUnrecognised`. It is never read as the lowest declared role, which would grant access nobody recorded, and the adapter does not normalise it on read for the same reason. A membership denial still outranks it, so an operator investigating a refusal is shown the cause they can act on. The role is checked in the Domain policy rather than by a database CHECK constraint: SQLite cannot add one to an existing table without rebuilding it, and a value written by a future deployment has to fail closed in the policy anyway.

**The role travels with the resolved business.** `BusinessMembershipResolution` carries the business id and the role together, so the two always come from one membership lookup and cannot disagree. `ICurrentBusinessProvider.RequireRoleAsync` is how the Application layer reads it, memoised per request exactly like the business id — so a role change applies on the member's next request, with no cache to wait for and no sign-out needed. The one-active-membership fail-closed rule is unchanged.

**One capability table.** `Inventory.Application.Access.RoleCapabilities` is the single role → capability definition, over the fifteen-capability `Capability` vocabulary (`Dashboard.View`, `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, `PickList.View`, `Inventory.Operate`, `Purchasing.Operate`, `Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults`, `Expenses.Manage`, `Reports.View`, `Imports.Run`, `SiteCommissions.Manage`, `Integration.Manage`, `Data.Repair`, `Members.Manage`, `Roles.View`, `Business.Manage`). An Operator holds the four operational ones; a Manager adds the financial, expense, import and commission work; an Owner adds the business's own configuration — integration, data repair, members, roles and the business record. Each role's set is written out in full, so the table reads the way the agreed table in #328 reads, and the hierarchy it happens to describe is asserted by a test rather than assumed by the code. There is no second table, no per-controller list and no capability derived from a role's stored value.

**Defining a capability is not enforcing one.** Issue #521 stores the role, publishes the vocabulary and reports it, and enforces nothing. Enforcement is [Capability authorization](#capability-authorization-issue-525) below, which reads `RoleCapabilities.Allows` so that what an endpoint enforces and what `GET /api/me/access` reports cannot drift apart.

**`GET /api/me/access`** returns the caller's role, that role's capability names, and their business's name and time zone (issue #499). It takes no parameter of any kind and describes the caller alone: no other member, no other business, and no identifier for either. One header changes what it *reports*, and only for one caller: a platform administrator's `X-Role-Preview` (issue #720) narrows the reported capability list to that list intersected with the previewed role's, so a Super Admin previewing an Operator is told exactly what an Operator would be told. The `role` field is unchanged by it — it is the caller's own stored role, and the preview changes what they may do rather than who they are — and nothing was added to the contract. See [Super Admin role preview](#super-admin-role-preview-issue-720). It carries the same `[Authorize]`, delegated-scope and membership requirements as every other business endpoint, and deliberately no capability requirement of its own — a member must be able to ask what they may do whatever role they hold. `GET /api/business/current` keeps its own contract (and since issue #525 requires `Dashboard.View`, which every role holds).

**A role only ever arrives from a reviewed path.** `bootstrap-business` accepts an optional `Role` name per configured member, validated against the same vocabulary and defaulting to `Owner` in the command's own options; an unrecognised name refuses the whole run and writes nothing. That default is the configuration's, not the entity's — the membership it writes always states a role (issue #679). Re-running never changes the role an existing member already holds, for the same reason it never resurrects a revoked approval. The additive migration backfilled every pre-existing membership to `Owner`, so no existing member's access changed. Changing a role afterwards is the Owner-only member management of issue #533, on one endpoint — `PUT /api/members/{membershipId}/role` — which accepts the role's published *name*, checked against this same vocabulary before anything is stored, and never a stored value; see [Member management](#member-management-list-role-revoke-and-reinstate-issue-533). That is still the only request path that writes a role onto a *membership*. One other path accepts a role from client input: creating an invite link (issue #531) records the role its redemption will grant, on the invite row rather than on a membership, and checks the submitted name against this same vocabulary in the same way — see [Invite links](#invite-links-create-list-and-cancel-issue-531). No endpoint anywhere accepts a stored role value.

#### Capability authorization (issue #525)

A role that nothing checks is a label. Issue #525 is where the capability table starts deciding requests: the everyday business endpoints declare the capability they need, and an architecture test stops a new endpoint from quietly defaulting to "every active member may call it". It is the first of #502's two enforcement slices; the Manager- and Owner-only controllers it deliberately left open are [issue #526](#capability-authorization-on-the-manager-and-owner-endpoints-issue-526) below, and the dashboard's financial redaction — the one capability that decides part of a *response* rather than an endpoint — is [issue #527](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527), extended to the site endpoints by [issue #697](#site-financial-redaction-issue-697), to the machine and product responses by [issue #698](#machine-and-product-financial-redaction-issue-698), and swept across every remaining Operator-readable endpoint by [issue #700](#operator-readable-financial-disclosure-issue-700), which holds the endpoint-by-endpoint classification table and the standing guard behind all four.

**Where it is enforced: the authorization middleware, from one table.** `InventoryApi.Auth.CapabilityPolicy` names one ASP.NET Core authorization policy per declared `Capability` (`Capability:Inventory.Operate`, and so on for all fifteen), `Program.cs` registers every one of them, and `BusinessCapabilityAuthorizationHandler` answers them all by asking `RoleCapabilities.Allows`. A controller or action declares one with `[RequireCapability(Capability.InventoryOperate)]`, which is an `AuthorizeAttribute` carrying that policy's name, so the decision is made by the authorization middleware before any action runs — not by a filter each controller has to remember, and not inside a use case. Every capability is registered even where no endpoint declares it yet, so #526 added attributes and nothing else, and the member-management issues will do the same. `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` is the one capability that is deliberately **not** an endpoint requirement: what a role without it may not see is a handful of figures inside responses every role may request, which an `AuthorizeAttribute` cannot express — see [Dashboard financial redaction](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527) and [Site financial redaction](#site-financial-redaction-issue-697).

**`Dashboard.ViewFinancials` now also governs every revenue, profit, margin, profitability-status and trend/comparison figure, and inventory value, on the Dashboard, Sites and Machines pages** (issue #699), not only the two figures #527 redacts in the Dashboard summary response. #699 itself is read on the frontend alone, from `AccessService.allows('Dashboard.ViewFinancials')` the same way every other hidden action in [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528) is, and a page-level hide is not a boundary on its own. The endpoints behind it have since become a boundary of their own. The **site** endpoints, `GET /api/sites` and `GET /api/sites/{id}/products`, send `null` for the three site revenue figures and the estimated card profit to a caller without the capability ([issue #697](#site-financial-redaction-issue-697)). The **machine and product** endpoints, `GET /api/machines`, `GET /api/machines/{id}`, `GET /api/machines/{id}/products`, `GET /api/products`, `GET /api/products/{id}` and the low-stock list, withhold their figures the same way (issue #698, see [Machine and product financial redaction](#machine-and-product-financial-redaction-issue-698)). The **stock-movement and purchasing** endpoints — `GET`/`POST /api/products/{id}/stock`, `GET /api/stock-history`, the `api/purchases` reads and writes and the `api/supplierorders` reads and create — withhold a movement's `inventoryValueAfter` and a line's nested product `inventoryValue` (issue #700, see [Operator-readable financial disclosure](#operator-readable-financial-disclosure-issue-700), which also classifies every remaining Operator-readable endpoint). Unit cost and site/machine selling price are unaffected throughout and stay visible to every role, as are a purchase's own costs and totals.

**Controllers reference capabilities, never roles.** Which roles hold a capability is `RoleCapabilities`'s single answer, and it is the same answer `GET /api/me/access` reports, so the API and the frontend's rendering decisions cannot disagree. An architecture test fails the build if any controller attribute names a `BusinessRole` at all.

**The role comes from the request's memoised membership resolution.** The handler resolves it through `ICurrentBusinessProvider` — the same per-request scoped provider `BusinessScopeMiddleware` uses — so the capability decision and the business the request then acts in come from one membership lookup and cannot disagree, and a role change applies on the member's next request exactly as it already did. Resolving it in the handler rather than reading a `BusinessScope` the middleware published is deliberate: `UseAuthorization()` runs **before** `UseMiddleware<BusinessScopeMiddleware>()`, so a policy that waited for the published scope would be able to pass before any membership had been checked. This is the same reasoning the diagnostics bypass follows in re-evaluating its own policy instead of inferring one from pipeline position. The order is stated in `Program.cs` and pinned by `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests`; the handler's independence from it is pinned by `BusinessCapabilityAuthorizationHandlerTests`.

**A support session is the second source of a capability, and the handler is read-only for it** (issue #551). Since #551 the handler asks `Inventory.Application.Access.CurrentCapabilities`, which is the one place that chooses between `RoleCapabilities` for a member and `SupportSessionAccessPolicy`'s fixed set for a platform administrator inside a support session; the support state itself comes from `ISupportSessionAccessor`, for the same ordering reason the role does not come from the published scope. In that state the handler additionally requires the request's method to be `GET` or `HEAD`, and that rule is checked first and independently: a write is refused as a write — `403` with `read_only_support_session`, whatever capability it carried — rather than as a missing capability. See [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**A role preview is a third input to that one answer, and it only ever subtracts** (issue #720). `CurrentCapabilities` now has a third per-request fact beside the membership and the support session: `IRolePreviewAccessor`, the role a platform administrator asked to be answered as in the `X-Role-Preview` header. Whichever of the two sources applies still decides what the request would have been allowed, and the preview is then **intersected** with the previewed role's own capabilities — so the base is the caller's own role outside a support session and the session's fixed set inside one, and a preview can never grant a capability the request did not already hold. Because this handler, `GET /api/me/access` and the financial redaction all ask that one class, none of them has a rule about previews. The read-only half is not in this handler, deliberately: it has to hold on the endpoints that declare no capability as well, so `RolePreviewMiddleware` applies it ahead of `UseAuthorization()`. The three refusals it makes — `role_preview_not_permitted` (`403`), `invalid_role_preview` (`400`) and `read_only_role_preview` (`403`), in that precedence, with a support session's own refusals between the second and the third — are described in [Super Admin role preview](#super-admin-role-preview-issue-720).

**A refusal is a bare `403`.** It names no capability, no role, and none of the roles that would have been allowed; the reason — which capability, which role, or that the membership did not resolve — is logged for an operator instead. The two support-session refusals of issue #551 are the single exception and are not an exception to the principle: `SupportSessionAuthorizationResultHandler` gives *only* a failure carrying one of those two codes a body, and that body carries the code and a fixed sentence and nothing else. Because authorization runs first, a caller with no usable membership gets that bare `403` on a capability endpoint rather than `BusinessScopeMiddleware`'s "not associated with a business" sentence, which is strictly less than they were told before; endpoints that declare no capability yet are unchanged, and `GET /api/me/account-state` remains the only place a caller learns their own account state. The handler fails closed in every direction: an unauthenticated caller, a membership that does not resolve for any reason (missing, revoked, ambiguous, a business whose lifecycle status is not `Active`, a stored role this deployment does not declare) and a member whose role simply does not grant the capability all leave the requirement unmet, and an unmet requirement is a refusal rather than a fallback to the least-privileged role.

**Requirements accumulate, so narrowing one action is additive.** A controller-level capability plus an action-level one means that action needs both. `SuppliersController` is the shape: every action needs `Purchasing.Operate`, and `PUT /api/suppliers/{id}/gst-defaults` additionally needs `Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults`, because a supplier default decides how later purchases are classified. Reading the defaults stays on `Purchasing.Operate` so an Operator recording a purchase can see which classification it will be given. Every role holding `Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults` holds `Purchasing.Operate` too, so the combination is the GST capability in effect and strictly narrower than either alone.

**What this slice applies.** `Dashboard.View` on `DashboardController` and `GET /api/business/current`; `PickList.View` on `PickListController`; `Inventory.Operate` on `ProductsController`, `CategoriesController`, `InventoryCountController`, `StockController`, `StockHistoryController`, `MachinesController` (Sync Restock included) and `SitesController`; `Purchasing.Operate` on `PurchasesController`, `SupplierOrdersController` and `SuppliersController`, with the supplier GST-default edit on `Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults`. Every role holds all of these except the GST-default edit, which an Operator does not — so for the single live business, whose every member is an Owner, nothing a member reaches changes.

**Four endpoint classes, and nothing else.** `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` (`backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Architecture/`) walks every action on every controller and recognises exactly four ways an endpoint may be authorized:

1. **A capability policy** — `[RequireCapability(...)]` on the action or its controller. This is what a business endpoint normally is.
2. **The platform-admin surface** — `PlatformAdminPolicy` *and* `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute` together (issue #336 for the read-only diagnostics API, #544 and #545 for the Super Admin businesses API, #550 for the support-session control endpoints: one class, one marker and one policy for all of them). Both halves are required, and such an endpoint declares no capability: `PlatformAdminPolicy` is satisfied by a configured Entra `(tid, oid)` pair that is deliberately not a membership row, so a capability there would be unsatisfiable for the only caller it exists for — and a diagnostics endpoint that declared one would be inviting a business role into a cross-business path. The test asserts both directions, and `CapabilityPolicyCompositionTests` asserts the policies themselves: `PlatformAdminPolicy` holds no capability requirement and no capability policy holds a platform-admin requirement.
3. **The membership-not-required family** — `MembershipNotRequiredEndpointAttribute` on an endpoint named in the allowlist the test now owns (issue #523; today `api/me/account-state`, `api/invites/redeem` and `api/onboarding/business-applications`, each added by its own reviewed change). `MembershipNotRequiredEndpointAllowlistTests` reads that same single list and keeps the assertions about what the marker may never remove.
4. **`GET /api/me/access`** — one endpoint, named explicitly rather than marked, because a marker would be a mechanism somebody could reuse. A member must be able to ask what they may do whatever role they hold.

The classes are asserted to be mutually exclusive, and that there are exactly four: a fifth would be a new way for an endpoint to be authorized, which is a decision to be made here and in that test together. The test also proves no public controller method escapes the rule by carrying no HTTP method attribute.

**There is no pending list.** Issue #525 left the twelve controllers it did not reach on a temporary `PendingClassification` list inside that test, as a named record of what was still open rather than an exemption. Issue #526 classified all twelve and **deleted the list**, so the rule above now holds for every action on every controller with no exception. There is nothing to add a controller to, and no such list may be reintroduced: a new endpoint fails the build until the same pull request decides what it requires.

**What proves this slice.** `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` (the role matrix through the real pipeline and the real migration history: three members holding the three roles against every endpoint this slice protects, the expected roles written out literally from #328's table rather than read back from `RoleCapabilities`; a non-member and an undeclared stored role refused everywhere; a refusal that leaks no part of the matrix; `401` still `401`; a role change applying on the next request; the ordering contrast with an endpoint that declares no capability; and one membership lookup for a request that both checks), `BusinessCapabilityAuthorizationHandlerTests` (the grant and refuse directions per role, every denial reason, no lookup for an anonymous caller, independence from the published scope, and two requirements answered independently), `CapabilityPolicyCompositionTests` (one policy per declared capability, each denying anonymous callers, the two policy families not deciding each other's questions, and the default policy unchanged), `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` (the four classes above) and `PlatformAdminAuthorizationTests`, where the configured platform administrator is still refused by every business endpoint — now over-determined, since they hold neither a membership nor any capability.

#### Capability authorization on the Manager and Owner endpoints (issue #526)

Issue #526 is #502's second and last enforcement slice. The twelve controllers #525 deliberately left on its `PendingClassification` list — the Manager-only financial surfaces, the Owner-only Nayax configuration and the five maintenance data repairs — now each declare the capability #328's agreed table gives them, and that list is gone. Nothing else changed: no new capability, no new policy, no schema change, no route, verb or response body, and no change to the one `RoleCapabilities` table. The mechanism is exactly the one described above; this subsection records *which capability each surface declares and why*.

**The matrix, by page and endpoint.** The capability was declared on the controller in every case of this slice, because every action of each of these surfaces needed the same one. Requirements accumulate down an endpoint, so a controller-level declaration is the narrowest honest statement when that is true, and no action-level override was added anywhere in #526 itself. The table is kept complete as endpoints are added: the member management of issue #533 and the invite links of issue #531 each followed the same shape — its own controller, one capability, and a row here in the same change. Two later reviewed edits — issue #548's business settings and issue #537's Nayax connection status read — declare per action instead, for the reason given under the table.

| Page | Endpoints | Capability | Operator | Manager | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Admin → Users (the page is issue #534, added by issue #531) | `api/members/invites` (create, list), `api/members/invites/{inviteId}/cancel` | `Members.Manage` | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |

Several of these endpoints additionally withhold a financial figure *inside* their response from a role without `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, which is a separate decision from the capability above and is not expressible as an attribute. The table of which figure on which endpoint is in [Operator-readable financial disclosure](#operator-readable-financial-disclosure-issue-700) (issue #700), which classifies every Operator-readable endpoint in one place rather than per row here.

The table's `Business.Manage` row was added by issue #548, which is the first endpoint to declare `Business.Manage`: the capability existed in the one role → capability table from issue #521 and nothing required it until an Owner could change the business record. Its read shares its write's capability, as the next paragraph's rule says a read normally does — the settings read reports the business's contact address, ABN and GST registration, which is the business's own tax and contact detail rather than anything a page needs to render. It is nevertheless one of the two rows whose controller holds a second, weaker rule: `GET api/business/current` on the same `BusinessController` keeps `Dashboard.View`, so both are declared per action and neither inherits the other. See [Business settings API](#business-settings-api-issue-548).

The other is `NayaxConnectionController` since issue #537: its test, save and re-test actions declare `Integration.Manage` and its status read declares `Dashboard.View`, each on the action, because the connection banners every member sees have to be able to ask whether Nayax is working (see [Saving a tested connection and re-testing it](#saving-a-tested-connection-and-re-testing-it-issue-537)). Both controllers are the same shape and the same reason: because requirements accumulate, a controller-level capability beside a weaker action-level one would silently require both, so where one controller's actions genuinely differ, every action declares its own.

**A read shares its surface's capability, with one deliberate exception.** `Expenses.Manage` covers the expense list and the attachment download as well as the writes, and `Reports.View` covers each report and its export: an export is the same figures in another container, and a separate capability for it would be a way to read a report that is otherwise refused. The one read/write split in the whole matrix stays #525's supplier GST defaults, because an Operator recording a purchase genuinely needs to see which classification it will be given. The site commission *report* is not split onto `Reports.View` either: it is the surface the agreements are maintained from, and a role that could read what a site is owed but not why would be shown a number it cannot check.

**A preview is as restricted as its apply.** All five repair controllers put `Data.Repair` on the controller, covering preview, dry run, history read and apply alike. A preview reads exactly the financial history its apply rewrites and returns the fingerprint or plan id the apply is authorised by, and on `api/sale-costing` the only difference between projecting the change and writing it is a `dryRun` flag. Restricting the apply while leaving the preview open would restrict nothing anybody cares about and hand every member the business's costing ledger. `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests.Every_action_of_a_repair_controller_requires_only_the_data_repair_capability` pins that none of them drifts onto a weaker capability later.

**The endpoints no page owns, and the reviewed reasoning for each.** Issue #526 says `NayaxSalesSyncController` and `DataQualityController` follow the page that calls them; issue #681 added the third entry, an action whose own page stopped calling it:

- `POST api/nayax-sales-sync` → **`Dashboard.View`**, and since issue #681 **`Inventory.Operate`** as well. The home Dashboard calls it on load, before Sites and Machines, so both sections calculate from one freshness boundary (issue #187). `Imports.Run` would leave an Operator's Dashboard refreshing nothing and reporting stale sales on every visit — the page broken for them rather than a decision anybody made. It surfaces no figure the Dashboard does not already show, and redacting those figures by role is [issue #527](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527) below.

  The second capability is there because **this endpoint writes**: it persists imported sales and rebuilds inventory costs for the products a completed sale touched. `Dashboard.View` is the read capability every role holds, including any future read-only role #328 anticipates (the Viewer), so an endpoint that writes under it alone is a hole waiting for that role to exist. `Inventory.Operate` is the capability declared because the write is an inventory one — the same capability Sync Restock's write carries — and because every role in the matrix that holds `Dashboard.View` also holds it, so **no current role's sync access changes**. Requirements accumulate, so the declaration narrows and never widens.

  It is also **rate-limited per business** since issue #681: `Inventory.Application.SalesSync.NayaxSalesSyncRateLimiter` allows ten runs per business per two minutes, claimed before the first Nayax call, and a refused run answers `429` with `Retry-After` and reaches neither Nayax nor the database. One run is one Nayax request per machine plus one, and the Dashboard triggers one per load — which a browser repeats on every visit, back-navigation and refresh — so this was the most expensive call in the application and the easiest to repeat, with nothing bounding either the requests against someone else's API or the write amplification in this one. The limit is per business rather than per actor for the reason the connection test's is: what it protects is the business's own Nayax account and its own rows. The window is kept in memory, like every other limiter here (docs § SQLite operating assumptions). Because the allowance is the business's, members opening the Dashboard together share it: ten simultaneous loads all synchronize (`NayaxSalesSyncControllerTests`), and a load past that is refused. A refusal proves the business started runs inside the last two minutes, so the Dashboard loads its persisted figures and says they were refreshed in the last couple of minutes, not that synchronization failed (`isSalesSyncRecentlyRefreshed`); any other error still shows the not-synchronized warning. The `429` body names no wait and points at `Retry-After`, because the wait can be up to the whole window.

- `GET api/products/inventory-value-summary` → **`Inventory.Operate` and `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`** (issue #681). It is an action on `ProductsController`, so it carries the catalogue's own capability; the second one is declared on the action. The endpoint reports the exact value of the business's inventory at cost, broken down — the figure [issue #527](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527) omits from the dashboard response entirely for a role without `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, today an Operator. On the catalogue's capability alone, that redaction was a presentation detail rather than a boundary: an Operator could read the number directly. No page calls this endpoint (`ProductService.getInventoryValuationSummary` has no caller since the dashboard stopped using it), so it was gated rather than removed — gating preserves the API contract, which AGENTS.md § Architecture rules asks for, while removing it would be a breaking change for a caller nobody has surveyed. A Manager and an Owner hold both capabilities and are unaffected; an Operator gets the ordinary bare `403`. Gating this one action left the figure reachable by summing the catalogue's own `inventoryValue`, which is what [issue #698](#machine-and-product-financial-redaction-issue-698) closed, along with the machine endpoints' revenue, profit and profitability-status figures: those endpoints stay on `Inventory.Operate` for every role, because an Operator restocks from them, and only the figures inside the response are withheld. [Issue #700](#operator-readable-financial-disclosure-issue-700) closed the last two routes to the same figure — a stock movement's `inventoryValueAfter` and the catalogue snapshot nested in a purchase or supplier-order line — and audited every other Operator-readable endpoint for one.
- `GET api/products/purchase-cost-summary` → **`Dashboard.ViewFinancials`**, so a Manager and an Owner (issue #788, B of parent #786). It reports what every product was last bought for and what it was cheapest at, with the supplier of each — supplier purchasing facts over the whole catalogue, which is the same kind of figure `GET api/products/{id}/price-history` shows one product at a time. **It is its own controller, `ProductPurchaseCostsController`, for exactly that reason**: a controller declares one capability for every action it holds, so adding this action to `ProductsController` would either have inherited the catalogue's `Inventory.Operate` — handing those figures to every role that may operate inventory — or, declared per action, left the catalogue and this read looking alike when they are not. The first page that calls it is the home Dashboard's Reorder Alerts table (issue #789, see [Provider-optional dashboard and Needs Ordering screens](#provider-optional-dashboard-and-needs-ordering-screens-issue-727)); Products → Needs Ordering (issue #790, D of #786) is the second, and All Products (issue #791, E of #786) the third, requesting it once for its listed product ids and showing the Last/Cheapest purchase columns only with `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`. The Angular client is `ProductPurchaseCostService`. It is read-only and `GET`, so a support session may call it under the central `GET`/`HEAD` rule of issue #551, which grants `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`. See [Supplier product price history and comparison](#supplier-product-price-history-and-comparison-issue-63).
- `GET api/data-quality/nayax-catalog-reconciliation` → **`Integration.Manage`**, so an Owner alone. **No page calls it**: nothing in `frontend/inventory-app/src` requests this route. "Follow the page" therefore has no answer, and leaving it unclassified would have kept it open to every member, so the capability follows what the endpoint *is* — a live, read-only report of how this business's Nayax catalogue has drifted from its local records (issue #55), read before deciding whether a mapping needs fixing. `Data.Repair` grants exactly the same roles today, so no role's access differs between the two readings; `Integration.Manage` was chosen because the endpoint reports on the integration and repairs nothing. A future Owner-facing integration page can show it with no change here.

**What an Operator and a Manager lose, and when.** An Operator can no longer reach expenses, any report or export, the imports, the site commission surface, the Nayax fee rates, the catalogue reconciliation or any repair. A Manager additionally cannot reach the Nayax fee rates, the catalogue reconciliation or any repair — a Manager may read a report whose underlying fee rate only an Owner may change, which is the agreed table and not a defect. Routes, verbs, request shapes and success responses are unchanged; the only new answer is the bare `403` an under-privileged caller receives. Every member of the one live business is an `Owner`, so nothing anybody reaches changes until non-Owner roles are assigned.

**Holding a capability is not a way across the business boundary.** The two decisions are separate and both in force: the capability says which *kind* of thing a member may do, and `AppDbContext`'s query filters plus `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` say *whose* data they may do it to. The Owner of one business holds every capability there is and still reads nothing of another business's — `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` proves it in both directions over two seeded businesses, and proves the order too: a role that does not hold the capability gets the policy's bare `403` rather than the boundary's `404`, so it is never told whether an id it may not use exists somewhere.

**One testing detail worth knowing.** `POST api/imports/nayax-sales`, `POST api/admin/nayax-sale-timestamp-repair/preview` and the multipart expense create/update overloads declare `[Consumes("multipart/form-data")]`. A declared content type is matched during **endpoint selection**, which runs *before* the authorization middleware, so a JSON body on one of those routes answers `415` for every caller whatever role they hold. A test that wants to assert anything about authorization there has to send a multipart body; the `415` reads no membership and leaks nothing.

**What proves this slice.** `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` — the four-class rule with no pending list, the same rule per controller, the 33 rows reading each Manager/Owner capability back off its route (#526's own 32, both page-following mappings included, plus issue #536's connection test added to the same theory as a reviewed edit), and the repair-controller rule above. `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` — every new surface in the role matrix, called as all three roles through the real pipeline and the real migration history with a second business present throughout; the write and apply actions in the one direction a test may assert without running them; a caller with no membership refused everywhere; and the three two-business isolation tests described above.

#### Dashboard financial redaction (issue #527)

Everything above decides whether a request is answered at all. `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` is the one capability that decides part of a *response*, and issue #527 is where it starts doing so: `GET /api/dashboard/summary` sent every member the week's sales and the inventory valuation, and the Dashboard is the landing page, so every role holds `Dashboard.View` and must keep reaching it. What an Operator may not see is two figures inside the body, which an endpoint attribute cannot express. [Issue #697](#site-financial-redaction-issue-697) applies the same decision to the site endpoints, [#698](#machine-and-product-financial-redaction-issue-698) to the machine and product ones, and [#700](#operator-readable-financial-disclosure-issue-700) to everything else an Operator can reach; everything below is about the Dashboard summary alone.

**Two published shapes, and the role picks one.** The summary now returns `Inventory.Application.Dashboard.IDashboardSummaryDto`, the union of exactly two types:

| Caller | Shape | Top-level properties | `inventory` properties |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Role grants `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` (Manager, Owner) | `DashboardSummaryDto` (unchanged) | `asOfUtc`, `businessDate`, `salesThisWeek`, `needsRefill`, `needsOrdering`, `inventory` | `inventoryValueAtCost`, `isInventoryValueComplete`, `productsWithUnknownCost`, `productCount`, `unitsInStorage` |
| Role does not (Operator) | `RedactedDashboardSummaryDto` | `asOfUtc`, `businessDate`, `needsRefill`, `needsOrdering`, `inventory` | `isInventoryValueComplete`, `productsWithUnknownCost`, `productCount`, `unitsInStorage` |

Nothing else differs: `asOfUtc`, `businessDate`, the refill and ordering cards and every remaining inventory figure are value-for-value what the same request produces for a Manager, and a Manager's and an Owner's response is byte-for-byte what it was before — no property added, renamed, retyped or removed.

Both shapes gained a third section state later, and neither is a role decision: a support session replaces the refill and ordering cards with `{ "available": false, "reason": "SupportView" }` (issue #552), and a business with no usable Nayax connection has its refill card replaced the same way while its ordering card carries a storage-only `mode` (issue #726, see [Provider-optional reorder and dashboard summary](#provider-optional-reorder-and-dashboard-summary-issue-726)). Redaction and provider availability are independent: one withholds money, the other withholds the machines.

**A redacted figure is absent, not `null` and not `0`.** That is why this is two types rather than one type with nullable properties and a "redacted" flag. `null` is *already* a meaningful answer for `inventoryValueAtCost` — "the valuation is incomplete, because some product's cost is unknown" ([Inventory Value tile](#dashboard-inventory-value-tile-issue-42)) — so reusing it for "you may not see this" would make an incomplete valuation and a withheld one indistinguishable. `0` would read as a known zero week, which is a financial statement about the business and a false one. A property the returned type does not have, finally, cannot be reintroduced by a later change to a serializer option, a converter or an attribute, and there is no flag anybody can forget to read. MVC serializes the object the action returned, so the absence is the type's shape rather than a serialization setting.

**The figures are not calculated for a caller who may not see them.** `GetDashboardSummary` resolves the caller's role first and, when the capability is absent, does not call `IDashboardSummarySalesFactsProvider` at all: there is no week-to-date query in that request, so nothing is read and then dropped. The inventory valuation needs no extra read either way — the redacted card is projected from the same single catalogue snapshot the non-financial cards already use, through the same `InventoryValuationPolicy` — so a redacted request makes two reads instead of three and no formula is duplicated.

**The decision is made in the use case, from the one capability table.** This is the deliberate exception to "capabilities are decided by the authorization middleware": the decision is about which figures are *read*, so it belongs where the reading happens. It still comes from `RoleCapabilities.Allows` — the one role → capability table `GET /api/me/access` reports from — through `ICurrentBusinessProvider`, the same per-request memoised membership resolution `BusinessCapabilityAuthorizationHandler` and `BusinessScopeMiddleware` read, so what the endpoint enforces, what the response contains and what the frontend was told cannot drift apart, and a role change applies on the member's next request. No role name appears in the decision. It fails closed: a caller whose membership does not resolve, for any denial reason, is refused with `BusinessAccessDeniedException` before anything is read, rather than being treated as the least-privileged role — unreachable through the endpoint, whose `Dashboard.View` policy refuses them first, and fail-closed if it ever were.

**The controller stays thin.** `DashboardController` keeps `[RequireCapability(Capability.DashboardView)]` exactly as #525 left it, returns whichever shape the use case built, and strips, recomputes and re-decides nothing. No endpoint's authorization class changed and nothing was added to `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests`. The Development-only Swagger document describes the union's common properties; the two concrete shapes are documented here rather than as an OpenAPI `oneOf`, because no generated client exists ([API documentation policy](#api-documentation-policy)).

**The Angular Dashboard renders the redacted shape since issue #528.** `DashboardSummary` in `models.ts` types `salesThisWeek` and `inventory.inventoryValueAtCost` as optional, and the page hides the "Sales this week" and "Inventory" cards when they are absent, rendering the two non-financial cards alone. It keys off the response rather than off the capability, so this API's decision stays the only one there is and no card can read a figure it was not given. An incomplete valuation (`inventoryValueAtCost: null`) is present, so that card stays and reports "Unavailable" as it always did; a still-loading or failed summary keeps all four cards, because not knowing a figure yet is not the same as having been told it is not this caller's to see. The fix was never for the API to send `null` instead. See [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528).

**What proves this slice.** `DashboardSummaryRedactionApiTests` (the exact serialized property sets through the real request pipeline and the real migration history, with three members of one business holding the three roles over one seeded fleet, catalogue and completed sale: an Operator's top-level and `inventory` sets, that neither property name nor either figure appears anywhere in their body, the full sets plus the seeded valuation for a Manager and an Owner, and an Operator's remaining figures matching a Manager's value for value) and `GetDashboardSummaryRedactionTests` (the decision over a fixed clock, with the roles written out literally from #328's table: the redacted shape for an Operator, zero calls to the sales port and no period handed to it, the non-financial figures identical to an Owner's, the incomplete-valuation flag and unknown-cost count surviving redaction, every figure for a Manager and an Owner, and every denial reason refused with nothing read). `GetDashboardSummaryTenancyTests` additionally covers, relationally, that an unresolved membership reads neither the sales, the catalogue nor the fleet.

#### Site financial redaction (issue #697)

Issue #527 above is the pattern; issue #697 is the same decision applied to the second surface that sent every member a financial figure. `SitesController` is gated by `Inventory.Operate`, which an Operator holds — stocking and pricing a site is day-to-day inventory work, and the page is how a person stocking machines reads what is in them — so `GET /api/sites` sent every member each site's `todayRevenue`, `currentWeekRevenue` and `previousComparableWeekRevenue`, and `GET /api/sites/{id}/products` sent them each product's `estimatedCardProfit`. The frontend-only hide of [issue #699](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528) kept those figures off the page but left them in the raw response, which is not a boundary; this slice is the boundary.

**What is withheld, and what deliberately is not.** The recorded decision (Cristhyan, 15 October 2026) is that `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` governs every sales, revenue, profit, margin, profitability-status, trend and inventory-value figure — and that **unit cost and selling price are not among them**. So `averageUnitCost` and `sitePrice` stay visible to every role, together with stock, `maxStock`, the MDB codes, the machine count and the low/empty alert counts, and only the four amounts below change:

| Caller | `GET /api/sites` per row | `GET /api/sites/{id}/products` per row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Role grants `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` (Manager, Owner), or a support session | `todayRevenue`, `currentWeekRevenue`, `previousComparableWeekRevenue` as calculated (unchanged) | `estimatedCardProfit` as calculated (unchanged) |
| Role does not (Operator) | all three `null` | `estimatedCardProfit` `null` |

**A withheld figure is `null`, and never `0`.** `0` would be a financial statement about the business and a false one: a site that took no card payment today genuinely reports `0` to a caller who may see it, so the two had to stay distinguishable and `null` is what means "not yours to see". This is deliberately *not* #527's two-types-per-shape treatment, for a reason that is about the contract rather than taste: both site endpoints return a JSON **array**, and MVC serializes each element by its declared element type, so a union of two record types inside a `List<T>` would either lose the extra properties or need a `$type` discriminator on the wire. The fields are therefore nullable on the one published `SiteSummaryDto`/`SiteProductDto`, which is what the issue's migration note specifies and what the frontend already accepts — #699 made every site revenue and profit field optional and nullable in `models.ts` and made every template show "Unavailable" rather than `$0.00` or `NaN`, which is why #699 had to merge first. `estimatedCardProfit` was already nullable for an estimate that could not be made (no priced mapping, no cost basis, no effective fee rate, ambiguous commission configuration), so for that one field `null` now carries two meanings; the page never shows the difference, because a role that may not see the estimate is shown no column at all.
