membership, so a refusal there goes to the dashboard rather than to any state in this table.

**The access-unavailable page names no business.** `BusinessDeactivated` says to contact the
business Owner, `MembershipAmbiguous` says to contact support, and `MembershipRevoked` says to
contact the Owner too, but is also the one state the backend's membership-resolution policy treats
as eligible under `GET /api/me/account-state`'s `onboardingEnabled` flag - so it is the one state
the page offers **I have an invite link** for unconditionally, and **Start a new business** for
only when `onboardingEnabled` is true, matching the API's own eligibility rule rather than a
frontend guess. Sign-out needs no control of its own here: the application shell's header carries
the one sign-out control on every route, this one included.

**The global `403` handler** (`memberForbiddenNoticeInterceptor`) shows "you don't have access to
this" through the toast every other failure already renders with, for any `403` from a member
endpoint - `classifyMemberRequest`, the same classification `accessForbiddenInterceptor` uses
([issue #528](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528)), so
the two interceptors cannot disagree about what counts as one. A `403` from
`GET /api/admin/diagnostics/access` is therefore silent on every route: that probe is the sidebar's
quiet platform-admin question (issue #335), its refusal is the expected answer for every ordinary
member, and it says nothing about a business membership. The two other platform-admin surfaces are
silent for the same reason — the support-session control endpoints, and (issue #673) the sidebar's
other quiet shell read, `GET /api/super-admin/businesses/pending-count`. It does not fire while the current route is
`/welcome`,
`/application-pending`, `/application-rejected`, `/access-unavailable` or `/invite/:token`
(`ACCOUNT_STATE_BYPASS_PATHS`, matched by prefix for the invite token): a person on one of them has
already been told, by the routing itself or by the page they are on, exactly what their situation
is, and the shell's own eager reads on those routes (the sidebar's `GET /api/me/access` among
them) would otherwise show a contradicting toast on top.

**Cache invalidation is #528's trigger set, applied to the account state too**
(`AccountStateService` and `account-state-forbidden.interceptor.ts`): sign-in, sign-out, an MSAL
active-account change, any `403` from a member endpoint other than `GET /api/me/account-state`
itself (a `403` from `GET /api/me/access` **is** included, because that read requires membership
and its own refusal is itself a staleness signal), window focus more than five minutes after the
last read, and an explicit `refresh()`. `AccountStateService` is a sibling cache to `AccessService`
built the same way, rather than a shared base the two refactor into, so #528's already-tested
caching logic is untouched by this slice.

**The refresh between the two caches runs one way only** (issue #602). `GET /api/me/access`'s own
refusal still refreshes the account state, for the reason above - a membership revoked while the tab
was open shows up there first - but `GET /api/me/account-state`'s refusal now refreshes **nothing**:
not the account state (it is this cache's own read) and not the capabilities either, which is the
exclusion that was missing. The two probes can therefore no longer refresh each other, so persistent
`403`s settle instead of alternating for as long as the tab is open; issue #528's classification
table above lists what each kind of refusal starts, and
`forbidden-interceptor-chain.spec.ts` asserts the exact request count the composed chain issues
before it goes quiet.

**The answer belongs to the identity signed in now** (issue #603), by the same rule and the same
mechanism [#528's section](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528)
states for the capability cache. An actual change of signed-in identity publishes `unread` again
before the new read is issued or waited for, so `accountStateGuard` and the shell's own business
lookup wait for the new person's state rather than routing the new account on the previous
account's `Member` (or `NoMembership`) answer; a late response from a read the change superseded —
including after rapid switches — is refused by the generation check, publishes nothing, and does
not clear the current read's pending state; a sign-out clears both answers with no authenticated
probe; and the MSAL account event and the settling interaction that both report one change read the
new identity once. A same-identity re-read keeps its own answer published while it runs. Pending is
still not the same thing as the current identity's `unavailable`: only the second one is the
documented fail-open case that lets a navigation through.

**The shell waits for the account state before any business call.** `AppComponent`'s existing
business lookup (issue #499, `GET /api/business/current`) now reads the cached account state
first and asks for the business only when it answers `Member` - an account with no usable
membership has no business to look up, and the call would only receive the same `403` every other
member endpoint already gives it. An account state that could not be read still attempts the
lookup, for the same fail-open reason the guard does: the endpoint itself remains the boundary.
Since issue #671 that skip has one exception and one consequence: it does not apply inside an
effective support view, where the business the request resolves is the session's and the
administrator may hold no membership of their own, and a *later* `Member` answer for the same
identity - an accepted invite, an approved application - makes the shell read the business it
skipped. See [Reloading the business time zone after a context
change](#reloading-the-business-time-zone-after-a-context-change-issue-671).

**And the state it waits for is the current identity's** (issue #604). The shell starts that lookup
afresh on the same account-change trigger these caches use (see [Application shell and
navigation](#application-shell-and-navigation-issue-391)), and the previous identity's answer has
already gone back to `unread` by then (issue #603), so a switched-to account is never granted a
business lookup - or refused one - by the previous account's `Member` or `NoMembership` answer.
`GET /api/business/current` is issued for the new identity once that identity's own state has
answered, exactly once, and not at all while it is still pending; the documented unavailable
fallback and the bounded retries are unchanged, and a late answer from the superseded read reaches
no shell decision at all.

**The shell also withholds the business navigation from a known nonmember** (issue #676). Until it
did, the sidebar was rendered independently of the account state and built its menu from the
capability answer alone — and that answer cannot tell these cases apart, because
`GET /api/me/access` answers `unavailable` for all of them: nobody signed in, a member whose probe
failed, and somebody whose membership the API has already refused. `unavailable` offers *every*
destination (the fail-open rule above), so a signed-out visitor and a known nonmember were offered
a full business menu whose every endpoint would refuse them. `access/business-navigation.ts` adds
the one rule that distinguishes them, from what only the shell knows:

| What the shell knows | Ordinary business navigation |
| --- | --- |
| Nobody signed in | Withheld — there is no account to be a member of, and every destination would answer `401` |
| An effective support view (`viewing`) | Offered, whatever the administrator's own state says: the session names the business the tab's requests resolve, the same exception issue #671 gives the business lookup |
| Account state `unread` | Withheld — nothing has been answered yet, the same rule the sidebar already follows for an unread capability set |
| Account state `Member` | Offered; which destinations is still the capability set's decision, fail-open answer included |
| Account state `NoMembership`, `ApplicationPending`, `ApplicationRejected`, `MembershipRevoked`, `BusinessDeactivated`, `MembershipAmbiguous` | Withheld — `BusinessScopeMiddleware` refuses every business call for them, and `accountStateGuard` routes each to the page that explains it |
| Account state `unavailable` | Offered — the documented fail-open case, unchanged: a failed probe must not strand a legitimate member |

`AppComponent` decides it (`businessNavigation`) and `SidebarNavComponent` renders it through
`navigationFor`'s third argument, which leaves the business destinations out **structurally** rather
than through an empty capability set, so a destination that declares no capability of its own cannot
leak into a withheld menu either. Three things are deliberately unchanged: `AccessService` still
fails open on its own unreadable answer and is not made to fail closed anywhere; the separately
authorized `Super Admin` group still follows `GET /api/admin/diagnostics/access` alone, so a
platform administrator with no business membership is offered that group and nothing else
(issue #546); and a tab that cannot present a support session still renders no routed page at all
(issue #668), with its own account state deciding its menu, because its requests resolve the
administrator's own membership. A changed identity withholds the menu from the moment it changes,
for the same reason issue #603 publishes `unread` again: the previous account's answer was somebody
else's. Like every other capability and account-state rendering rule here, **this hides a menu
rather than protecting a page.**

**What proves this slice.** `account-state.service.spec.ts` (mirroring `access.service.spec.ts`:
the cached read, every refresh trigger, the unknown-state fallback, a superseded answer discarded,
and issue #603's shared identity-change suite from `identity-cache.spec-helpers.ts`, asserted
against this cache too - the previous answer dropped before the new read answers, a subscriber
arriving mid-read answered from the new identity, rapid switches, a previous identity answering
last, one read for the duplicated MSAL notifications, a sign-out with a read in flight, and a
same-identity refresh keeping its own answer), `account-state.guard.spec.ts` (routing for
every state, the fail-open answer, reading once for several navigations, and waiting for the new
account instead of routing on the previous account's state),
`access-unavailable.component.spec.ts` (the per-state
message, naming no business, and the revoked page with onboarding on - both options - and off -
invite only), `account-state-forbidden.interceptor.spec.ts` and
`member-forbidden-notice.interceptor.spec.ts` (the respective `403` triggers and the bypass-route
list, including that a `403` on a bypassed route never shows the generic notice and that the
diagnostics probe is silent on an ordinary one), `forbidden-interceptor-chain.spec.ts` (the three
interceptors composed over the real caches: persistent probe refusals settling at an asserted
request count, the one-way refresh, and the preserved notice and suppression), and
`app.routes.spec.ts`/`app.component.spec.ts` (`accountStateGuard`'s position on every business
route, the five bypass routes, and the shell asking for no business before the account state is
known). Issue #676's withheld navigation adds `business-navigation.spec.ts` (the rule for signed
out, unread, every published nonmember state, `Member`, the unreadable account state and an
effective support view), the real shell rendering the real sidebar in `app.component.spec.ts` (each
of those states, a `Member` whose capability probe failed keeping every destination, an identity
transition withholding the menu until the new state answers, a platform-only administrator keeping
`Super Admin` alone, an effective support view, and a tab that cannot present a session), and
`sidebar-nav.component.spec.ts`/`navigation.spec.ts` (a withheld menu rendering no destination for
an unreadable capability set while an offered one still renders them all).

### Admin Users page (issue #534)

`/admin/users`, one slice of #505 (under #328): where an Owner manages their business's people and
invite links from one page. It is the first Angular caller of issue #533's four member-management
endpoints and issue #531's three invite endpoints - both only read the capability answer this page's
route already gates on (`Members.Manage`, `app.routes.ts`), and both refuse every other caller
themselves regardless of what this page renders.

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `components/admin/users/admin-users.component.ts` | `AdminUsersComponent`: the routed page, composition only - it lays out the two sections below and owns no state or service call of its own |
| `components/admin/users/member-management.component.ts` | `MemberManagementComponent`: the Members section - the roster, the role-change control, and the revoke/reinstate actions, each behind a confirmation |
| `components/admin/users/member-invites.component.ts` | `MemberInvitesComponent`: the Invites section - creation, the once-only link display with its Copy button, the list by status, and cancellation |
| `services/member.service.ts` | `MemberService`: the four `/api/members` calls, and `BUSINESS_ROLES`, the three published role names mirrored for the role-change and invite-creation dropdowns |
| `services/member-invite.service.ts` | `MemberInviteService`: the three `/api/members/invites` calls |

**Composition, not a grown page.** Per [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191), the Members and Invites sections are each a distinct workflow with its own substantial UI, state, actions and error lifecycle, so each is its own feature component injecting its own service - the same shape `NayaxConnectionWizardComponent` composes into the Integrations page - rather than two sets of state grown directly into `AdminUsersComponent`.

**Every refusal is shown exactly as the API phrases it.** Neither section interprets, reworks or duplicates a membership rule: a role change or revocation that would leave the business with no active Owner, a reinstatement of someone who has since joined another business, a role change on a revoked membership, and a cancellation of a used or expired invite are all `409` sentences read from `error.error.message` (the `ProblemDetails` extension `DomainExceptionHandler` writes) and shown through the toast unchanged - see [Member management](#member-management-list-role-revoke-and-reinstate-issue-533) and [Invite links](#invite-links-create-list-and-cancel-issue-531) for what each sentence is. The confirmation dialog before a role change, a revoke, a reinstate or a cancel is a safety prompt only; the server's own rule, re-checked under its write lock, is what actually decides the request.

**The role control displays this component's own state, so an unsaved role can never stay on screen.** The native `<select>` moves to the chosen option the moment the Owner picks it, before the confirmation dialog has been answered and before the server has seen the request, so what the control displays is `MemberManagementComponent`'s own `selectedRoles` state (keyed by membership id) and not `member.role`. Cancelling the confirmation, and any failure of the role change - the last-Owner `409` included - puts that state back to the server-confirmed `member.role`, and a confirmed change records the role the response returned. Binding the control one-way to `member.role` instead could not do this: the bound expression never changes when the server refuses a change, so Angular would not re-touch the DOM, the control would keep showing a role the server rejected right next to the toast refusing it, and re-choosing the same role would raise no `change` event to retry with. The server remains the only authority on what a role actually is; this state is what the Owner is looking at.

**The selection lives on each `<option>`, not on the `<select>` itself (issue #678).** A combined implementation review of 15 October 2026 flagged a hypothesis: `[value]` on the `<select>` was assigned while the `@for` block below it was still creating the `<option>` elements, which is a real Angular update-order hazard rather than a theoretical one. A regression test confirmed it - a `Manager` or `Operator` row's native `select.value` read back as `Owner` (the first declared role) immediately after the asynchronous member load, even though `displayedRole()` returned the right role throughout, because Angular's update pass set the `<select>`'s own `value` property before the `@for` repeater had written each `<option>`'s `value`, so the browser's selection search found no match yet and kept the first option's default selection. The fix moves the selection onto each `<option>`'s own `[selected]="role === displayedRole(member)"` binding (and `[selected]="!displayedRole(member)"` on the disabled `Unknown` option for a member with no role yet), so Angular sets each option's selectedness directly on that option once it exists, with no value search and no dependency on instruction order between the `<select>` and its `@for` content.

**The invite link is composed here, once, and kept nowhere else.** `MemberInviteService.create` returns the token exactly once, on the same terms `InviteRedemptionService` documents for the redemption side; `MemberInvitesComponent` builds the link as `${window.location.origin}/invite/${token}` - the API has no authoritative knowledge of the web application's address - holds it only in the component's own `justCreated` field, and clears that field when the Owner dismisses it or creates another invite. Copying follows the same clipboard-with-fallback shape as the Nayax connection wizard's support-request copy ([The Nayax connection wizard](#the-nayax-connection-wizard-issue-538)): `navigator.clipboard.writeText` when available, and a toast pointing at the selectable field when it is not.

**What this slice does not do.** No bulk member or invite actions, no audit-event view, and no business-settings editing - those are other pages. Redeeming an invite is the separate `/invite/:token` page ([Invite acceptance page](#invite-acceptance-page-issue-535)), and there is no email sending, so the Owner delivers the composed link themselves.

**What proves this slice.** `member.service.spec.ts` and `member-invite.service.spec.ts` (every call, its URL and body, and the API base URL join), `member-management.component.spec.ts` (the roster rendered, the load error and empty states, a role change and a revoke and a reinstate each requiring confirmation and calling nothing until confirmed, a cancelled confirmation calling nothing, an unchanged role prompting nothing, the last-Owner and already-a-member refusals shown verbatim, and the selected option itself asserted at the DOM level - the native `select.value` and its selected option's label read back correctly for an Owner, a Manager and an Operator row immediately after the asynchronous member load and again after the list is reloaded with a different role (issue #678, where this assertion is what caught the ordering defect above), the disabled `Unknown` option selected for a member with no role, reverting to the stored role after a cancelled and after a refused role change, with the refusal toast kept and the same selection retryable afterwards, and keeping the new role once the API confirms it), `member-invites.component.spec.ts` (the list rendered, the load error and empty states, a role required before creation, the created link shown once with its expiry and copied to the clipboard or falling back to manual selection, the link dismissed on Done, a pending cancellation requiring confirmation, and the API's own refusal shown verbatim for a refused creation or cancellation), and `admin-users.component.spec.ts` (the page composing both sections).

### Invite acceptance page (issue #535)

`/invite/:token` carried `OnboardingPlaceholderComponent` until this slice of #505 (under #328)
replaced it with `InviteAcceptanceComponent`: where an invited person who opens their link, signs
in if needed, joins the business with one click. The redemption endpoint it calls,
`POST /api/invites/redeem`, is issue #532's ([Invite redemption](#invite-redemption-issue-532));
this slice is the one caller `frontend/inventory-app/src` has for it.

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `access/invite-acceptance.component.ts` | `InviteAcceptanceComponent`, at `/invite`: takes the tab's pending invite token into memory, decides Accept-button vs. redirect from the cached account state, calls the redemption endpoint, and refreshes both caches before landing on the dashboard |
| `access/invite-address-bar.guard.ts` | `inviteTokenAddressBarGuard` (issue #681): `/invite/:token`'s `canMatch` guard, which hands the token to the pending invite, strips it from the address bar and redirects to `/invite` before `MsalGuard` runs; `pendingInviteTokenGuard`, which matches the acceptance page at `/invite` only while a pending invite exists; and `INVITE_ADDRESS_BAR_ROUTE` |
| `access/pending-invite-token.ts` | The pending invite (issue #681): the token held in this tab's `sessionStorage` through a sign-in redirect, read and removed in one step, expiring after 15 minutes |
| `access/invite-link-reopen.component.ts` | `InviteLinkReopenComponent` (issue #681): the tokenless `/invite` page, telling a person who reloads or returns to it to open their invite link again |
| `access/invite-redemption.service.ts` | `InviteRedemptionService`: the one `POST /api/invites/redeem` call, with the token in the request body and nothing else |
| `access/account-state.guard.ts` | Gained `REDEEMABLE_ACCOUNT_STATES` and `nonRedeemableAccountStateDestination`, alongside `ACCOUNT_STATE_ROUTE` |

**The token never reaches the address bar's history, `MsalGuard` or MSAL (issue #681).**
`/invite/:token` never activates. Its `canMatch` guard, `inviteTokenAddressBarGuard`, runs during
route recognition, before any `canActivate` guard: it hands the token to the tab's pending invite
(`access/pending-invite-token.ts`), rewrites the current history entry to `/invite` with
`history.replaceState` when the address bar shows the link, and redirects the navigation to
`/invite`. The acceptance page is matched at `/invite` only while a pending invite exists
(`pendingInviteTokenGuard`), so `MsalGuard` only ever runs on `/invite`. A signed-out visitor's
sign-in redirect therefore starts from, is stored by MSAL as, and returns to `/invite`: the token is
not in MSAL's redirect start page or its `localStorage` cache (`auth-config.ts`), not in a history
entry Back returns to, and not in the page address a `Referer` could be built from. The history
rewrite is the guard's, not the router's, because the router updates the address bar only after a
navigation's guards pass, and a signed-out visitor's `MsalGuard` leaves the page before that. An
in-app navigation from the welcome page's invite field never put the token in the address bar, so
the guard leaves that page's own history entry alone.

**The pending invite is the one place the token waits.** Before the review of PR #696 the token
crossed the sign-in round trip inside MSAL's redirect start page, which MSAL keeps in
`localStorage` (shared by every tab and kept after the tab closes) until the redirect lands; that
was a copy this application neither controlled nor cleared. The pending invite is narrower:
`sessionStorage`, so one tab only and gone when the tab closes, never sent to any server, removed by
`InviteAcceptanceComponent.ngOnInit` in the same step that reads it into a component field, and
treated as absent (and removed) once it is more than 15 minutes old, so an abandoned sign-in does
not leave an invite waiting. A browser that refuses storage loses the hand-off and shows the
`/invite` page below. After `ngOnInit`, the token is held only in memory and never written to a
cookie, a log line or an error report, and `InviteRedemptionService` sends it only in this one
request's JSON body, never in a URL path or query string, so no HTTP or router logging of a request
or route *URL* can ever carry it either. The token is single-use, expires after seven days, and is
stored only as a hash on the server (`MemberInviteToken.Hash`,
[Invite redemption](#invite-redemption-issue-532)).

**The tokenless `/invite` explains itself (issue #681).** Once the page has taken the pending
invite, a reload of `/invite` or a Back into it matches the second `/invite` route,
`InviteLinkReopenComponent`, which says to open the invite link again and offers the home page,
instead of falling through to the `'**'` wildcard and landing on the dashboard or the welcome page
with no explanation. It carries no guard, like the public `auth` route, because it makes no request
at all, and `memberForbiddenNoticeInterceptor` treats `/invite` as one of its bypass routes.
`invite-address-bar.guard.spec.ts` drives a signed-out visitor through the application's real
route table, with `MsalGuard` replaced by a stand-in that starts the login redirect from the
router state's URL: the address bar reads `/invite` when the redirect starts, the redirect start
page is `/invite` too, nothing is written to `localStorage`, and the invite page reached after
sign-in redeems the token and empties the pending invite. `pending-invite-token.spec.ts` covers
the read-once, expiry and refused-storage rules, and `invite-link-reopen.component.spec.ts` pins
the tokenless route and its text.

**Eligibility is read from the cached account state, never assumed.**
`REDEEMABLE_ACCOUNT_STATES` — `NoMembership`, `MembershipRevoked` and `ApplicationRejected` —
mirrors the backend's `MembershipEligibility.AllowsActiveMembership` ([Invite
redemption](#invite-redemption-issue-532)): the three states that hold no active membership of
their own are the three the component offers the Accept button to, and an account state that could
not be read (`AccountStateService`'s own fail-open `unavailable` answer) is treated the same way,
for the same reason `accountStateGuard` fails open — the redemption endpoint re-checks eligibility
itself and is the one answer that counts. Every other state — `Member`, `ApplicationPending`,
`BusinessDeactivated` and `MembershipAmbiguous` — is sent straight to the page its own state
already calls for, through `nonRedeemableAccountStateDestination`: `Member` to the dashboard,
every other one to `ACCOUNT_STATE_ROUTE`'s existing destination, rather than showing a button the
API would only refuse.

**The API's refusal is shown exactly as it is written.** `InviteRedemptionService` does not
interpret the response body beyond the one field a successful redemption carries; a refusal's text
comes from `error.error.message`, the `ProblemDetails` extension `DomainExceptionHandler` already
writes, so the one generic unusable-invite sentence (expired, used, cancelled, invalid, or an
undeclared role — [Invite redemption](#invite-redemption-issue-532)), the already-a-member
conflict, and the deactivated-business release sentence each render verbatim rather than being
reworded or guessed at by this component. A refusal with no readable message (a non-domain error)
falls back to one generic sentence this component owns, and leaves the Accept button enabled again
so the attempt can be retried.

**Acceptance re-reads both caches, in order, before it lands anywhere.** On a successful
redemption, `AccountStateService.refresh()` and then `AccessService.refresh()` are chained and
awaited — not fired without waiting for either to answer — before the one navigation to `/`: by the
time it runs, the dashboard's own `accountStateGuard` and capability guard read the caller's new
`Member` state and granted capabilities already published, rather than the stale pre-redemption
answer either cache would still be holding if the navigation ran first.

**What this slice does not do.** No invite preview before acceptance (the redemption endpoint
takes a token and returns only the granted role — there is nothing to preview), the Users page
(#534's task), and the first-sign-in "start a new business" choice (#508's tasks).

**What proves this slice.** `invite-acceptance.component.spec.ts` (the token stripped from the
address bar before anything else, never written to a Storage API or a cookie, the token surviving
in memory through to redemption, the Accept button for each redeemable state and fail-open for an
unreadable one, a successful redemption for a `MembershipRevoked` and an `ApplicationRejected`
caller, every other state sent to its own page instead of a `Member` to the dashboard, the two
cache refreshes awaited in order before the dashboard navigation, each API refusal's message shown
verbatim, the generic fallback for an unreadable refusal, and a failed attempt leaving the button
enabled again), `invite-redemption.service.spec.ts` (the token posted in the body and never the
URL, and the response's one field), the `REDEEMABLE_ACCOUNT_STATES`/
`nonRedeemableAccountStateDestination` cases added to `account-state.guard.spec.ts`, and
`app.routes.spec.ts` (the route now loads `InviteAcceptanceComponent`, still behind `MsalGuard`
alone).

### Welcome, pending approval and rejected pages (issue #542)

`/welcome`, `/application-pending` and `/application-rejected` - the three remaining
account-state routing destinations `accountStateGuard` carries (issue #529) - each carried
`OnboardingPlaceholderComponent` until this slice of #508 (under #328) replaced it with its own
page. The application form behind "Start a new business" and "Apply again" is #543's, described in
[Business application form](#business-application-form-issue-543).

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `access/welcome.component.ts` | `WelcomeComponent`: the `NoMembership` destination - the invite-link entry point, and, when `onboardingEnabled` is true, the start-a-new-business choice |
| `access/application-pending.component.ts` | `ApplicationPendingComponent`: the `ApplicationPending` destination - explains the review is pending, and its "check again" button re-reads the account state |
| `access/application-rejected.component.ts` | `ApplicationRejectedComponent`: the `ApplicationRejected` destination - the Super Admin's recorded reason when there is one, the same invite-link entry point, and, when `onboardingEnabled` is true, the apply-again choice |
| `access/invite-link-token.ts` | `extractInviteToken`: pulls the token out of a pasted `/invite/<token>` link or a bare token, shared by the welcome and rejected pages |

**I have an invite link reuses the invite acceptance route (#535) rather than redeeming anything
itself.** Both pages hold a pasted value only in their own field, extract a token from it with
`extractInviteToken`, and navigate to `/invite/<token>` on Continue - `InviteAcceptanceComponent` is
still the one caller of the redemption endpoint and the one place that decides whether a token is
actually usable. Opening the link directly, from an email or elsewhere, reaches that same route
without ever landing on either of these pages, so nothing further is needed for that case.

**Start a new business and Apply again are gated on onboarding.** Both are gated on the same
`onboardingEnabled` flag `GET /api/me/account-state` reports, matching the deployment's own
eligibility rule rather than a frontend guess - the same rule `AccessUnavailableComponent` already
follows for a `MembershipRevoked` caller. This slice shipped them without a destination; #543 made
each a link to the application form at `/apply`.

**Check again re-reads the account state, never assumes an outcome.**
`ApplicationPendingComponent`'s button calls `AccountStateService.refresh()`: a still-
`ApplicationPending` answer stays on the page with a reminder that nothing has changed yet, an
`unavailable` answer (the fail-open case every account-state read shares) shows a retry message
rather than guessing, and any other known state navigates to the page
`nonRedeemableAccountStateDestination` already names for it (`account-state.guard.ts`) - the same
helper `InviteAcceptanceComponent` uses, now with a second caller. A `Member` answer runs
`AccessService.refresh()` and waits for it before navigating to `/`, exactly as
`InviteAcceptanceComponent` does after a redemption, so the dashboard's own capability guard reads
the caller's freshly granted Owner capabilities rather than the stale pre-approval answer either
cache would still be holding if the navigation ran first.

**The rejected page shows the Super Admin's own recorded reason, verbatim, when there is one.**
`rejectionReason` is the one field `GET /api/me/account-state` carries for `ApplicationRejected`
(issue #523); a submission with none recorded falls back to one generic sentence this page owns
instead of inventing a reason the API never gave.

**What this slice does not do.** The application form itself (#543's, below) and its wiring from
these pages, and anything backend - this is a frontend-only slice over the existing
`GET /api/me/account-state` and `/invite/:token` routes.

**What proves this slice.** `invite-link-token.spec.ts` (the token extracted from a full link, a
path-only link, a bare token, and surrounding whitespace, and `null` for blank input),
`welcome.component.spec.ts` and `application-rejected.component.spec.ts` (the invite-link option
always offered and the start-a-new-business/apply-again choice shown only when `onboardingEnabled`
is true, the rejected page's recorded reason and its generic fallback, and a pasted link or token
navigating to `/invite/<token>`), `application-pending.component.spec.ts` (the still-pending
message, the fail-open retry message for an unreadable re-read, navigation to every other state's
own page, and the access-cache refresh awaited before the dashboard navigation once approved), and
`app.routes.spec.ts` (each route now loading its own component instead of
`OnboardingPlaceholderComponent`, still behind `MsalGuard` alone).

### Business application form (issue #543)

`/apply` is the form a signed-in person with no active membership fills in to apply to start a
business, over `POST /api/onboarding/business-applications` (issue #541). The welcome page's
"Start a new business", the rejected page's "Apply again" and the access-unavailable page's
"Start a new business" for a revoked member all link to it, each only when `onboardingEnabled` is
true.

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `access/business-application.component.ts` | `BusinessApplicationComponent`: the form, who may see it, the submit flow and how each refusal is shown |
| `access/business-application-rules.ts` | The inline validation: the API's rules and sentences for the name, contact email, ABN, GST registration and time zone, and the request body built from a valid draft |
| `access/business-application.service.ts` | `BusinessApplicationService`: the one `POST`, interpreting no refusal itself |

**Who may see it follows the API's eligibility rule.** The route carries `MsalGuard` alone and no
`accountStateGuard`, for the reason every account-state destination does, and
`ACCOUNT_STATE_BYPASS_PATHS` includes it so a stray member `403` shows no toast there. The page
itself reads the account state once: `REDEEMABLE_ACCOUNT_STATES` (`NoMembership`,
`MembershipRevoked`, `ApplicationRejected` - the API's `MembershipEligibility.AllowsActiveMembership`)
see the form while `onboardingEnabled` is true, and any other known answer is sent to
`nonRedeemableAccountStateDestination`'s page. An unreadable account state shows the form, the same
fail-open rule as `accountStateGuard`: the endpoint re-checks eligibility and its answer counts.

**The form's rules are copies of the API's, and the API stays authoritative.**
`business-application-rules.ts` mirrors `BusinessSettingsPolicy`, `AustralianBusinessNumber` and
`BusinessContactEmail` and reuses their sentences word for word, so the form and the `400` it
guards against never describe one rule two ways. The one difference is the time zone: the API
requires a non-blank IANA id, and the form also asks the browser's `Intl` whether it knows the id,
so a typo is caught before submitting. The ABN is optional and a blank one is sent as `null`;
GST registration has no default and must be answered yes or no. A field's message shows once it
has been left or a submit was attempted. The contact address starts as the signed-in account's own,
from the first sign-in claim (`preferred_username`, `email`, then the account's username) that is a
valid address, and stays editable.

**A recorded application lands on the pending page only after the account state is re-read.**
`AccountStateService.refresh()` runs before navigating to `/application-pending`, so the routes
behind it see `ApplicationPending` rather than the state the person applied from. A refusal stays
on the form: the API's own sentence for a `400` or `409` (`message`) and a `429` (`detail`), one
sentence of the page's own for the bare `404` a disabled deployment returns, and a generic one for
anything else.

**What this slice does not do.** Anything backend, the approval page (#510) and the approval
decision (#509).

**What proves this slice.** `business-application-rules.spec.ts` (each rule's accepted and refused
values, the API's sentences, and the request body), `business-application.service.spec.ts` (the
URL and body), `business-application.component.spec.ts` (the form for each eligible state and for
an unreadable state, the redirect for each ineligible state and for onboarding off, the email
prefill, when field errors appear, a successful submit refreshing the account state before landing
on the pending page, and each refusal's message), the welcome, rejected and access-unavailable
specs (each link pointing at `/apply`), `member-forbidden-notice.interceptor.spec.ts` (`/apply` is a
bypass route) and `app.routes.spec.ts` (`/apply` behind `MsalGuard` alone).

### Breadcrumbs (issue #457)

A shared breadcrumb renders once, in `app.component.html` immediately above `<router-outlet>`, so
it sits above every routed page's own `.page-title` without any page template rendering its own
copy. Three files own it, alongside the shell files above:

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `layout/breadcrumbs/breadcrumb-routes.ts` | The route → label/parent mapping (`breadcrumbRoutes`) and the pure `buildBreadcrumbTrail`/`buildTrailFrom` that turn a URL into a trail |
| `layout/breadcrumbs/breadcrumb.service.ts` | `BreadcrumbService`: the one live label a routed page may contribute from data it already loaded, reset to `null` on every `NavigationStart` |
| `layout/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs.component.ts` | Renders the trail for the router's current URL, recomputed on every `NavigationEnd` and on `BreadcrumbService`'s label |

**Metadata, not URL splitting.** `breadcrumb-routes.ts` is a small, explicit mapping — the same
convention `layout/navigation.ts` uses for the sidebar — of each nested route pattern (for example
`/machines/:id`) to a current-page label and an optional `parent` (`{ label, path? }`). It is
deliberately a separate mapping from `primaryNavigation`: the sidebar's `Products`/`Purchases`/
`Reports`/`Admin` groups are headings that are not themselves a route, while a breadcrumb parent
must be the real page that owns the child route (`/products`, `/purchases`, `/reports`, `/admin`,
`/machines`, `/sites`), so the two metadata sets name the same areas without being interchangeable.
A route with no entry — every top-level list page, the Dashboard, and the two URLs that load the
cross-cutting global Stock History page (`/stock-history`, `/products/:id/stock`, see [Routing and
loading](#routing-and-loading)) — renders no breadcrumb: `buildBreadcrumbTrail` returns an empty
trail for an unmapped URL and for an entry with no `parent`, because a one-item trail adds no
hierarchy. Nothing here ever derives a label by splitting the URL or reading browser history.

**Links, text, and the current page.** A parent with a `path` renders as a real `routerLink`; a
`parent` entry with no `path` renders as plain, non-link text — the "non-routable group" case the
acceptance criteria asks the mapping to support, exercised today only by a constructed fixture in
`breadcrumb-routes.spec.ts` because every current parent (`Products`, `Machines`, `Sites`,
`Purchases`, `Reports`, `Admin`) happens to have a real landing route. The current page is always
the trail's last item, is always plain text, and is the only item ever carrying
`aria-current="page"`; `BreadcrumbsComponent` never routes a `current` item through `routerLink`
even when the matched entry also has a `path`. Authorization is unaffected: every parent `path` is
an existing route already behind `MsalGuard` and its own API authorization, exactly as a sidebar
link is, so a breadcrumb exposes no name or route a guard would otherwise hide, and bypasses no
guard, because it only ever links to a destination that was already reachable.

**The live label, and why it cannot leak.** `/machines/:id` is today's one dynamic entry
(`dynamic: true`): `MachineDetailComponent` calls `BreadcrumbService.setCurrentPageLabel(machine
?.machineName ?? null)` from inside the same `machine$` pipeline its template already subscribes
to through `| async` — one `tap`, zero extra requests. `BreadcrumbsComponent` shows that live label
only while it is non-null and the matched entry is `dynamic`; otherwise it shows the entry's static
`label` (`Machine details` here), which is what covers both the initial load and a failed load.
Because `BreadcrumbService` resets the label to `null` on every `Router` `NavigationStart`, moving
from `/machines/5` to `/machines/9` on the same reused `MachineDetailComponent` instance shows
`Machine details` again the instant navigation starts, never `5`'s stale name, until `9`'s own
`machine$` emission supplies the new one. `/sites/:id/products` and the `/purchases/new` "receiving
a supplier order" variant stay on their static labels for now — `dynamic` is available to either
without touching `BreadcrumbsComponent` if a future issue asks for it.

**Responsive behaviour.** Every current trail is exactly two items (parent, current): no mapped
route is nested more than one level below a page that itself has no further parent. "Shorten a long
trail to the immediate parent plus current page" is therefore already the full trail, and
`.breadcrumb-list` (`styles.scss`) uses `flex-wrap` rather than a forced single line, so a long
label wraps onto a second line at a narrow width instead of causing horizontal overflow or being cut
off — nothing is hidden or ellipsized, so the full label stays in the accessible tree and visible at
every width. A third breadcrumb level, if one is ever needed, would need `buildTrailFrom` to return
more than two items and a collapsing rule for which middle item to hide first; neither exists yet
because no current route needs it.

**Semantics.** The root element is one `nav[aria-label="Breadcrumb"]` landmark holding an `<ol>`;
each separator is a `span[aria-hidden="true"]` between list items, never read by assistive
technology. A parent link is a real `<a routerLink>`, so it is keyboard-operable and picks up the
same global `:focus-visible` outline every other link uses (see [Application shell and
navigation](#application-shell-and-navigation-issue-391) and `styles.scss`); nothing here needs a
bespoke focus style.

### Shared provider availability and error-versus-empty states (issue #728)

Child E1 of issue #329 (decision P9), after the dashboard's own answer in
[issue #727](#provider-optional-dashboard-and-needs-ordering-screens-issue-727). It gives the
frontend **one** answer to "is this business's Nayax connection usable", **one** handling path for
the `409` that says it is not, and it stops five screens presenting a failed machine or site request
as an empty list. It is frontend only: no endpoint, no contract and no rule of its own.

**`ProviderAvailabilityService` is the one answer, read once per session.**
`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/provider/provider-availability.service.ts` calls
`GET /api/settings/nayax-connection/status` (`Dashboard.View`, so every role may read it) and shares
the result (`shareReplay`, the same shape `BusinessService` uses for the current business): however
many banners, filters and forms want it, the endpoint is asked a single time. `load()` emits only a
**settled** answer, so no screen renders a decision that has not been made. A read that failed emits
`unknown` and drops the shared attempt, so the next screen asks again.

**`load()` answers once; `watch()` keeps answering.** `load()` completes, which is what a page
resolving its own state or a route guard asking per navigation wants. A surface that stays mounted
across a reconnect — the sidebar of
[issue #729](#provider-locked-navigation-issue-729) — subscribes with `watch()` instead and is told
again every time this session's answer changes: a state `accept`ed, a refusal retained by
`noteRefusal`, a context forgotten by `reset`. Without it such a surface would hold the answer read
when it was created while the guards had already moved on, and one destination would have two
verdicts. Observing a change is **not** a second probe: `accept` and `noteRefusal` state the new
answer themselves, so only `reset` — which says this is a different business — makes the next ask
read the status again, and that read is still the one shared read. `watch()` emits `undefined`
before the first answer settles and again while a change is being answered, so a subscriber shows
the fail-open state rather than the previous business's locks while the new answer is on its way.

**The answer has one overall state and one state per feature.** `ProviderConnection` is `usable`,
`needsAttention`, `notConnected` or `unknown`. `providerConnectionOf` is a translation of
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionStatusGate` and not a second opinion - `Ready` and
`PendingPermissions` are the two usable states because that gate says so, and a status name this
build has never heard of is `unknown` rather than usable, for the same reason the gate is an
allow-list.

Keeping `needsAttention` apart from `notConnected` is the whole reason the overall state exists:
the two mean opposite things to a business, and collapsing them would withhold the Nayax fee category
from a business that does pay a Nayax monthly fee.

**A usable connection is never read as "every feature is granted".** A connection is usable in
`PendingPermissions` *precisely because* the business's Nayax account may have granted some reads and
refused others, so the overall state cannot answer for a feature. `ProviderFeature`
(`provider/provider-feature-permissions.ts`) is therefore a vocabulary of **kinds of Nayax read**,
not of pages, taken from the reads this application already declares in
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionCheck`:

| Feature | What it is | Declared check that is evidence about it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `machineFleet` | the operator's machine list and the site list derived from it (`GET /api/machines`, `GET /api/sites`, the pick list) | `Machines` |
| `machineSales` | a machine's latest sales read from Nayax | `MachineLastSales` |
| `machineStock` | a machine's own product/stock state | `MachineProducts` |
| `productCatalogue` | the operator's product catalogue and product groups | `ProductCatalogue`, `ProductGroups` |
| `providerRecords` | what only needs Nayax to be *part of* this business and makes no live read at all: the "Nayax Sync Restock" source of an already-recorded movement, the "Nayax monthly fee" expense category | none - no permission can be granted or refused for it |

`PROVIDER_FEATURE_CHECKS` is that mapping, and it is the feature-to-permission mapping issue #729
(E2) reads for a locked menu item. A check no feature claims - `SignIn`, which is about the
credentials rather than about a read, and `Machine` and `MachineLastAlerts`, which no screen depends
on - is evidence about nothing here rather than about the feature it most resembles.

Every feature then carries one `ProviderFeatureAvailability`, and the four states are answers rather
than labels on each other:

| Feature state | When |
| --- | --- |
| `available` | the connection allows the feature **and** evidence says Nayax granted the read |
| `notConnected` | the connection cannot serve it at all: `notConnected`, or `needsAttention` for a live read. `providerRecords` survives `needsAttention`, because stored credentials that stopped working are still a Nayax account the business pays for |
| `permissionNotGranted` | the credentials work and Nayax has refused this feature's read for lack of permission |
| `unknown` | nothing has stated it: the status is unread or unreadable, or the connection is usable and no test, re-test or refusal has said anything about this feature's permission |

`providerFeatureOffered` **fails open on `unknown`**, matching the banner and issue #727: withholding
a connected business's machine filter because one probe failed, or because nothing has yet stated a
permission, is a worse error than showing a filter whose own request then reports its own failure.
Only a *stated* refusal withholds a feature, and it withholds that feature alone - the connection's
own availability and every other feature are untouched, so a granted machine read stays usable beside
a refused sales read.

**Permission evidence is only ever evidence this application produced.** There are exactly two
sources, and neither is the status:

- **A completed connection test or re-test** (issues #536, #538). `providerPermissionsOfChecks` reads
  its check lines: a check refused with `PermissionNotGranted` is `denied` and outweighs a sibling
  that passed (a feature needing two reads needs both), a check that passed is `granted`, and
  everything else - `NotChecked`, an invalid token, a Nayax outage, an answer nobody interpreted -
  leaves the feature `unknown`, because a read nobody completed says nothing about a permission.
- **A `409 nayax_permission_not_granted` the session saw**, retained by `noteRefusal` against the
  feature whose request earned it. The refusal does not name a feature itself - the response carries
  the stable code and no operation name - so the caller passes the feature it was asking about, which
  is why `noteRefusal` takes one.

**The connection changes in exactly one place, so that is the one place the signal is refreshed.**
`NayaxConnectionWizardComponent` calls `accept(state, checks?)` with the state the server returned
from its status read, its save and its re-test (issues #537, #538), which replaces the shared answer
without spending another request. A save and a re-test pass the completed run's **check lines** - for
a save, the test whose draft it promoted, because the stored pair is exactly the pair that was tested
- so the per-feature answers are refreshed from them; a plain status read carries none, and then the
permission evidence is **cleared** rather than carried over onto a connection that may have changed.
`reset()` drops the status and every permission for a change of the business this tab resolves - a
support-session start, end or expiry - called from `SupportSessionService.applyBusinessContextChange`
beside `BusinessService.reset()` (issues #669, #670), because the cached answer is about one
business's connection and a support view resolves no Nayax credentials at all (issue #551).

**Bounded dependency: no contract reports a per-feature permission, or names one.**
`GET /api/settings/nayax-connection/status` publishes a status and `machineChecksPending` and nothing
per read, and `NayaxConnectionExceptionHandler` deliberately keeps
`NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException.Operation` out of the `409` body (it is logged server-side). So
in an ordinary session every feature is `unknown` until a request is refused, and only an Owner with
`Integration.Manage` can produce positive evidence, by running the rate-limited re-test. Two things
therefore cannot be built on this signal as it stands, and neither is invented here:

- a page that states up front which Nayax permissions a business is missing, without first being
  refused;
- issue #729's "waiting for Nayax permission (naming the missing permission)" wording. The
  application knows its own check names, not the Nayax permission an operator has to grant, and a
  name nothing published must not be guessed. Issue #729 therefore names the refused **read** and
  its endpoint - the only authoritative name there is - and prints no permission key; its own
  record states what Nayax's documentation does and does not publish, and what naming the key
  would need. See [Provider-locked navigation](#provider-locked-navigation-issue-729).

Closing either needs a backend contract change - the status response (or a new read) publishing each
declared check's last outcome, and an authoritative Nayax statement of the permission behind it -
which is a reviewed decision of its own, not an implementation detail of this signal.

**`noteRefusal(error, feature)` is the one HTTP handling path for the two `409` availability codes.**
It returns the `NayaxUnavailability` a refusal stated (`nayax_not_connected` /
`nayax_permission_not_granted`, worded by `provider/nayax-availability.ts` since issue #727) and
`null` for every other failure - a transport failure, a `502` from a real Nayax outage, a `403` about
the caller's own access - which stays an **error**, because reporting one of those as "Nayax is not
connected" would describe a connection nobody tested, and recording one as a permission refusal would
withhold a feature nobody refused. A not-connected refusal **replaces** the shared answer, taking the
status out of the refusal's own `nayaxConnectionStatus` extension (issue #520): the one `409` covers
"nothing stored" and "stored and known not to work" alike, so the code on its own cannot tell them
apart, and a refusal that published no recognised status records nothing rather than guessing. A
permission refusal instead records `denied` for the one feature it was about and leaves the
connection's own availability exactly as it was, because the credentials are working.

**`loadProviderList` is the one machine/site list load**
(`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/provider/provider-list-load.ts`). It reads the shared answer, does
**not send** a request the provider cannot answer, and reports exactly one of three outcomes that a
page may never confuse:

| Outcome | When | What a page does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `listed` | the request answered | render the control; an empty list is a legitimate empty list |
| `unavailable` | the shared answer refuses the feature - the connection cannot serve it, or this session has already seen Nayax refuse it for lack of permission - or the request came back with one of the two `409` codes | **hide** the control - a filter over a list that cannot exist is not a filter |
| `failed` | anything else | render an **error in place of** the control |

A feature the shared answer already refuses is not requested again, and the answer it carries says
which refusal it was: a connection that cannot serve the feature carries the not-connected answer
(the one the server itself would have given), and a retained permission refusal carries the
permission answer, so a page that has been told why says why.

Before this, each page subscribed to `MachineService.getAll()` and assigned `[]` on failure - or, on
the Pick List, had no error handler at all - so a refused request, a transport failure and a business
with no machines were all presented as the same thing: an empty dropdown that silently widens what
the page reports on.

**Where it is used, and what each screen hides.**

- **Pick List** (`PickListComponent`) is entirely a live fleet read, so `unavailable` replaces the
  machine selection, the "Selected Machines" card and the matrix with the one
  `nayaxUnavailableMessage` sentence for "The pick list". "No machines selected yet" and "Select at
  least one machine to build a pick list" are claims about this business's *selection*, not about
  Nayax. A `failed` machine read says so instead.
- **Report filters** (`ReportFiltersComponent` over `ReportPageBase`, plus
  `TransactionSalesReportComponent`, which does not extend it) hide the Machine select when there are
  no machines to filter by and show `machinesError` in its place when the read failed. Apply keeps its
  right alignment either way. **Site Commissions** does the same for its Site select over
  `SiteService.getAll()`, which is a live fleet read too.
- **Stock History** (`StockHistoryPageComponent`) keeps only the **"Nayax Sync Restock" source**
  option on this signal, through `providerRecords`, because the movements it selects are already
  recorded locally; the table keeps labelling a Nayax-sourced movement whatever the filter offers. Its
  **machine** filter left this signal in issue #746 - it is the business's own machine records now
  (see [Machine fields from the business's own machines](#machine-fields-from-the-businesss-own-machines-issue-746)).
- **The stock adjustment form** (`StockAdjustmentFormComponent`) takes its machine list from the page
  as an input and is no longer on this signal either (issue #746). It keeps the rule the signal
  taught: a failed read is an error in place of the field, never an empty one.
- **Expenses** (`OperatingExpenseComponent`) is on this signal for its categories and its wording
  only: without `providerRecords` it stops offering "Nayax monthly fee" for a **new** expense and
  drops the Nayax sentence from its subtitle. An expense already recorded under that category
  **keeps** it - in the table, in the Category filter and on the edit form, which offers the category
  whenever the expense being edited carries it - because a recorded expense is a fact about the past
  and this page must never quietly reclassify one. Its machine field and its list's machine filter are
  the business's own machines (issue #746).

**What is deliberately not here.** The home Dashboard and Needs Ordering keep issue #727's own
answer, derived from the summary and the reorder listing they already fetch: those responses are
authoritative about the cards beside them, and a second probe would be a second answer that could
disagree with them. Local machines are issues #740 (G1), #741 (G2) and #746 (G2b), the last of which
took three of the screens below off this signal. The menu was
issue #729 (E2), and it reads this signal through
[Provider-locked navigation](#provider-locked-navigation-issue-729).

**What proves it.** `provider/provider-availability.service.spec.ts` covers the status derivation,
the one-read-per-session cache, the retry after a failed read, the four per-feature states, a usable
connection claiming no permission, one granted feature beside one refused feature, the refusal
retained against one feature only, the refresh after a re-test, the clearing after a connection state
with no checks, the business-context reset, and every refusal `noteRefusal` must and must not claim
an answer for - including the transport failure that must never become permission evidence.
`provider/provider-feature-permissions.spec.ts` covers the feature-to-check mapping and the evidence
rule: a refused read outweighing a passed sibling, and `NotChecked`, a non-permission failure and a
check no feature claims all leaving a feature `unknown`.
`provider/provider-list-load.spec.ts` covers the three outcomes, the request that is not sent, the
per-feature difference between `machineFleet` and `providerRecords`, the second request a retained
permission refusal prevents while an unrelated feature stays loadable, and the failures that stay
errors.
`pick-list.component.provider-optional.spec.ts` and `reports/report-provider-optional.spec.ts`
cover each screen's hidden control, its error state, and the empty list neither may be confused with;
`stock-history-page.component.provider-optional.spec.ts` and
`operating-expense.component.provider-optional.spec.ts` cover what is left of this signal on those
two screens after issue #746 - the source option, the Nayax fee category and the subtitle;
`nayax-connection-wizard.component.spec.ts` covers the signal being refreshed by a save and a
re-test, including the per-feature permissions a re-test found, granted and refused alike;
`nayax-status-banner.component.spec.ts` covers three banners costing one read; and
`support-session.service.spec.ts` covers the answer being forgotten on a context transition.

### Provider-locked navigation (issue #729)

Child E2 of issue #329 (decision P6), after [the shared availability signal of issue
#728](#shared-provider-availability-and-error-versus-empty-states-issue-728). It puts that one
answer in the menu, so the application says which features need a sales provider **before** a page
has to. It is frontend only: no endpoint, no contract and no rule of its own, and every answer it
renders comes from `ProviderAvailabilityService`.

**The order is the statement.** `primaryNavigation` is: `Dashboard`, `Pick List`, `Machines`, the
`Inventory` group, `Purchases`, `Expenses`, `Reports`, `Admin` — everything that works with no
provider at all — then one `NavSectionHeading` ("Needs Nayax") and the live provider destinations
under it: `Sites` and `Site Commissions`. A heading is a heading, not a
control: it toggles nothing, links nowhere, renders as an `<h2>` over the entries after it, and
`navigationFor` drops it when every entry under it was left out, because a heading over nothing
claims a section this member does not have.

**`Machines` left that section in issue #740**, which is the only change to this design since. A
business keeps [its own machine records](#local-machines-and-external-machine-ids-issue-740) now, so
the destination always has something to show and its own create/rename/deactivate actions to offer:
the entry declares no `lockedWithout`, is never locked, and `/machines` carries no `requireProvider`
guard. The page withholds its own live stock, revenue and sync parts while the provider cannot serve
them, which is a decision about one page's content rather than about whether a destination exists.
The machine **details** route keeps its guard, because every panel on it is a Nayax read.

**Two renames, and one name per destination.** The `Products` group is `Inventory` (decision P11),
because it holds the whole of the business's own stock keeping, all of which works without a
provider; the Products **page** inside it keeps its own name, its URL and its breadcrumb. `Nayax
Settings` is `Integrations`, in the sidebar, on the `/admin` hub card and in the page's own heading
and breadcrumb — one destination with one name — and its URL (`/admin/nayax-settings`) is unchanged.
Every other breadcrumb is untouched: a breadcrumb parent is the real page that owns a child route,
and a sidebar group heading is not a page, so renaming a group and moving the site commission report
into its own menu section change no trail (`breadcrumb-routes.spec.ts`).

**Two declarations on a `NavLink`, because the two cases are not the same.**

| Declaration | What it means | What the menu does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lockedWithout: ProviderFeature` | the destination's page is a live Nayax read | shown **locked** while the shared answer refuses that read, and its route redirects to the "needs a provider" page |
| `hiddenWithoutProvider: true` | a provider repair or admin tool | left out of the menu entirely until the connection is usable |

Locking rather than hiding is the point for the first: a page an operator could have used, and could
use again by connecting Nayax, has to stay visible and explain itself. Hiding is right for the
second — Admin → `Imports` (the Nayax sales and settlement imports) and Admin → `Nayax Sale
Timestamp Repair` — because with no provider there is nothing of the provider's to import or repair,
so a locked entry would offer a tool for data that does not exist. `Integrations` carries neither: it
is where a connection is made, so it can never depend on one. The costing and GST repairs carry
neither either — they are the business's own data.

**`provider/provider-lock.ts` is the one place that answer becomes a verdict about a destination**,
and it holds nothing but pure functions, because the menu, the route guard and the page the guard
redirects to must agree about one destination. A menu that locked a page which then opened, or a page
that refused an entry the menu offered, is what that separation prevents.

| Function | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `providerLockOf(availability)` | `open`, `connect` or `permission` - `providerFeatureOffered` with the refused case split in two |
| `providerToolsOffered(connection)` | whether the repair and admin tools are offered: `usable` or `unknown` |
| `providerFeatureReadLabels(feature)` | the declared Nayax reads that feature needs, each named with its endpoint |
| `providerLockSummary` / `providerLockSentence` | the one line a locked entry carries, and the sentence its page shows |

`connect` and `permission` are kept apart for the reason issue #728 keeps `notConnected` and
`permissionNotGranted` apart: they need opposite things from an operator. Telling somebody whose
credentials work that Nayax is not connected sends them to re-enter a token that was never the
problem. And `unknown` is `open`, for the same fail-open reason the banners and the filters offer a
feature nothing has refused: a status probe that failed must not lock a page whose own request would
have answered it, so an unread status locks nothing and withholds no repair tool.

**Capability rules apply first.** `navigationFor` filters by capability and only then by the provider
answer, so an entry the role may not see stays **hidden** rather than becoming a locked advertisement
for a page that role never had. On the routes, `requireProvider` is declared **after**
`requireCapability` for the same reason: a member whose role does not include `/reports/site-commissions`
reaches the "access not allowed" page, not an invitation to connect a provider they still could not
use.

**Historical reports are never locked** (decision P5). Bookkeeping, Daily, Transactions,
Reconciliation, machine profitability, product profitability, GST and the reporting dashboard read
**stored** data, so they stay in the `Reports` group, carry no provider guard on their routes at all,
and report their own availability states instead (issues #730 and #731). Previously imported sales
stay readable after a disconnect. The site commission report is the one report in the provider
section, and it is not an exception: a site is known only from the live fleet read's `CustomerID`, so
with no usable provider it has no sites to report on and the API itself answers `isAvailable: false`
(see [Site commissions](#site-commissions) in AGENTS.md and issue #731). Its breadcrumb still names
`Reports` as its parent page, because `/reports` is still the page that owns that route.

**`requireProvider(feature)` is the URL half of a locked entry** (`provider/provider-lock.guard.ts`),
and it is presentation exactly as `requireCapability` is: every endpoint behind these pages resolves
the business's own Nayax credentials and answers `409` itself, whatever the router did. What the
guard changes is that typing `/machines` with no provider reaches one explanation instead of a page
of refusals, so the menu entry and the URL behave identically. It carries the refused URL to the page
as the `from` query parameter, which decides nothing: the page resolves the destination from the
declared navigation through `activeNavLink` and re-reads the availability answer itself, so a URL
somebody typed cannot make it say a page is locked when it is not.

**`ProviderLockedComponent` (`/needs-provider`) explains, and never refuses.** Like
`/access-not-allowed` it is where a guard *sends* somebody, so it declares no capability of its own -
the destinations that redirect to it need different ones, each already checked - and it is never a
dead end: it links to the Dashboard and says what still works without a provider. The two locks read
differently, which is the whole reason they are separate states:

- **`connect`** - "Machines is unavailable because Nayax is not connected", with a **Connect** button
  to `/admin/nayax-settings` for a member who holds `Integration.Manage`, and "Ask the business Owner
  to connect Nayax" for one who does not, rather than a dead button.
- **`permission`** - "Machines is waiting for a Nayax permission", the connection stated as working,
  and the refused read named with its endpoint: "Machine list (GET machines)". **No Connect button**,
  because re-entering credentials that already work fixes nothing; the action is to have the
  permission granted and then re-test on Integrations.

**What is named, and what is deliberately not.** Issue #729 asks for the permission message to name
the missing permission. What exists to name is the **read**: `PROVIDER_FEATURE_CHECKS` (issue #728)
maps a feature to the reads this application declares in
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionCheck`, and `provider/nayax-read-areas.ts` words each one with
its endpoint. That file is the **one** vocabulary for naming a refused Nayax area, shared with the
Owner's connection checklist and support request (issue #538), which is why it moved out of
`nayax-connection-checklist.component.ts` and is re-exported from there: two wordings for one refusal
is how a screen ends up asking Nayax for the wrong permission.

The Nayax permission **key** behind one of these reads is not printed, because nothing published
states it. Nayax's own developer documentation publishes a permission key and OAuth scope per
endpoint for its three dashboard-widget report endpoints only (`lynx_report_get_widgets`,
`lynx_report_get_widget_data`, `lynx_report_get_widget`), and for none of the five reads this
application depends on — `GET machines`, `GET machines/{id}/machineProducts`,
`GET machines/{id}/lastSales`, `GET operators/{operatorId}/products`,
`GET operators/{operatorId}/productGroups`; its app-tokens page documents only the *format* of a
scope (`{domain}:{action}`) with examples. The server does not say which operation was refused either
— `NayaxConnectionExceptionHandler` deliberately keeps
`NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException.Operation` out of the `409` body. So naming the Nayax permission
would mean guessing a name, which [issue #728's own
record](#shared-provider-availability-and-error-versus-empty-states-issue-728) already refused and
which AGENTS.md § Nayax contract verification forbids. Naming the read and its endpoint is the
authoritative thing this application can say, and it is what a support request to Nayax has to ask
for. Printing the permission key needs a published Nayax statement of it, and is a reviewed decision
of its own.

**One shared read, and none at all without a business.** `SidebarNavComponent` subscribes to
`ProviderAvailabilityService.watch()` only while the shell says the business navigation is `offered`:
a signed-out visitor and an account with no usable membership resolve no business, so there is no
connection to read a status for. That subscription is deliberately **its own**, beside the existing
`combineLatest` over the access answers rather than another arm of it - the provider answer changes
what the menu renders and nothing else, and re-asking the platform-admin probe or the
pending-applications count because a connection status settled would be one extra request per page
load. It starts `undefined`, so the menu renders immediately and locks nothing until the answer
settles. A locked entry keeps its `routerLink` and is **marked, not disabled**: clicking it is how an
operator reaches the explanation, so it carries a visible `Locked` badge, the lock sentence as its
`title` and the same sentence for a screen reader, and no `aria-disabled` - which would be untrue of
a link that does navigate.

**The menu follows the answer for as long as it is mounted.** It `watch`es rather than `load`s
because the sidebar outlives the answer: an Owner who saves working credentials on `Integrations`,
loses them, has one read refused by a page's own request, or starts a support session on another
business never leaves this component, and `requireProvider` asks again on every navigation. A menu
built from the answer read at mount would go on locking what now works - or offering a repair tool
for a provider that is gone - and disagree with the route and the locked page about the same
destination, which is exactly the agreement `provider-lock.ts` exists to guarantee. Following the
answer costs no extra probe (see
[`watch()`](#shared-provider-availability-and-error-versus-empty-states-issue-728)); only a context
reset reads a status, for the business the tab now resolves.

**What proves it.** `provider/provider-lock.spec.ts` covers every lock state, the fail-open `unknown`,
the tools gate over all four connection states, the read labels and both sentences.
`layout/navigation.spec.ts` covers the declared order and the section, the `Inventory` rename with
Products keeping its own name, the live provider destinations and the reports that are never locked
(including the machine profitability report that shares the `Machines` label), each lock state per
status and per role, the per-feature case where one refused read locks its destinations and leaves a
granted one open, the repair tools hidden and offered, the group dropped when the provider's was its
only child, and the capability rule applying first. `layout/sidebar-nav.component.spec.ts` covers the
rendered section heading, a locked entry still being a link with its badge and sentence, the
permission lock's own wording, the reports linked and unlocked with no provider, the hidden repair
tools, the one status read however many entries depend on it, and the read never made for a withheld
business menu; its `provider changes while it stays mounted` block proves the same sidebar - never a
recreated one - unlocks and offers the tools when a connection is accepted, locks them and withdraws
the tools when the credentials stop working, locks a destination as a *permission* when a refusal is
retained for its read, renders the new business's answer after a context reset, and reaches the same
verdict as `requireProvider` before and after the change.
`provider/provider-availability.service.spec.ts` covers `watch()` itself: the settled answer after
the nothing-known one, each kind of change told to a subscriber already listening, no second probe
for an accepted state, nothing said twice for a refusal already retained, the one new read for a
context reset, and `load()` still completing for a caller that asks once. `provider/provider-lock.guard.spec.ts` covers the URL half: the page opening, each
refusal redirecting with the exact refused URL, a detail URL, the granted sibling read, and the
unreadable status that opens the page. `provider/provider-locked.component.spec.ts` covers both
messages, the Connect button offered and withheld, the named read, the destination resolved from a
detail URL, the page opened with no destination, and the answer re-read rather than taken from the
URL. `app.routes.spec.ts` covers the guard order on every live provider route and its absence from
every report over stored data. `layout/breadcrumbs/breadcrumb-routes.spec.ts` covers the trails that
did not change and the one label that did.

### Target feature boundaries

Keep Angular standalone and migrate incrementally toward feature-local code:

```text
src/app/
├── core/
│   ├── config/                    Runtime configuration
│   └── http/                      Cross-cutting HTTP concerns only
├── layout/                            Application shell and navigation (started, issue #391)
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/                        Reusable presentation components
│   └── formatting/                Presentation-only helpers
├── features/
│   ├── products/
│   │   ├── pages/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── data-access/
│   │   └── models/
│   ├── stock/
│   ├── purchases/
│   ├── machines/
│   ├── sites/
│   ├── expenses/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── reports/
│       ├── shared/                Filters and report-page behavior
│       ├── bookkeeping/
│       ├── reconciliation/
│       └── profitability/
├── app.config.ts
└── app.routes.ts
```

This is a direction, not a required big-bang move. Move a feature when it is being changed, keep each move behavior-preserving, and avoid empty abstraction folders.

Use these ownership rules:

- **Pages** read route/query parameters, coordinate loading and mutation state, and compose the view.
- **Presentational components** receive typed inputs and emit user intent. They do not fetch unrelated application data.
- **Feature data-access services** own HTTP calls and transport mapping for one feature. They do not calculate financial results already supplied by the API.
- **Feature models** describe API contracts and view-specific types for that feature. Promote a type to `shared` only when multiple features genuinely use the same meaning.
- **Core services** are limited to application-wide infrastructure such as configuration and HTTP concerns. `core` is not a home for miscellaneous business logic.
- **The backend** remains authoritative for stock transitions, historical COGS, fees, commissions, reconciliation, and report calculations.

### Page composition boundary (issue #191)

Page and detail components (the components routed directly in `app.routes.ts`, whether via the
eager `component:` property or `loadComponent`) are primarily composition/orchestration
boundaries: they read route/query parameters, hold the page's own loading/error/selection state,
call feature data-access services for the page's own data, and lay out child components. They are
not the place for every new workflow to accumulate.

When a new piece of UI is a **distinct workflow** with its own substantial UI, plus its own
state, actions, and loading/error lifecycle (for example, a dialog with its own open/close state
that previews data, lets the operator make selections, and calls an API to apply them), implement
it as a dedicated feature component rather than adding it directly to the page component. This is
a responsibility/architecture rule, not a line-count limit: a page that is long because it lays
out many small, focused pieces of composition is fine; a page that owns a second workflow's
dialog state, API calls, and notifications alongside its own is the pattern to avoid, however
short that added code looks in a diff.

The preferred parent/child interaction is `@Input`/`@Output`, not a shared service or two-way
binding built for this purpose:

- **Inputs** pass the required context the child needs (for example, `[machineId]`).
- **Outputs** notify the parent only of a meaningful change that requires it to refresh or
  coordinate (for example, `(restockApplied)`); the child does not reach back into the parent's
  state or services to do this itself.

The Sync Restock workflow on `MachineDetailComponent` is the worked example this rule
generalizes; see [Nayax machine-stock event import and Sync Restock reconciliation (issue
#183)](#nayax-machine-stock-event-import-and-sync-restock-reconciliation-issue-183), "Frontend",
for the full description of `MachineRestockSyncComponent` and how `MachineDetailComponent`
composes it.

**Automated guard.** `frontend/inventory-app/src/app/architecture/page-composition.guard.ts`
